According to Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman, via The Verge, third-party apps stay on a paired iPhone, and the two devices handle requests together. Developers don’t build separate glasses apps; they enable Siri in existing iPhone apps through App Intents. Only recent iPhones will work, and there won’t be any Android support.

Gurman reports Apple envisions restaurant reservations through OpenTable, rides through Uber or Lyft, Starbucks orders, Amazon shopping, and Fandango tickets. Built-in functions cover Visual Intelligence, notifications, messages, calendar, reminders, music, and smart home control.

The glasses have Wi-Fi, so certain functions outside third-party apps keep working when the iPhone isn’t nearby. Apple is also stressing sound quality, which employees have called industry-leading, with support for phone calls, music, and FaceTime audio. Employees reportedly describe the product as “AirPods for your face”; camera-equipped AirPods are a separate product.

The prototypes, codenamed N50, run a pared-down version of visionOS on a new processor based on Apple’s older smartwatch chips. They’re slightly thinner than Meta’s second-generation Ray-Ban glasses, with cameras in oval openings that sit flush with the frame and a front status light. A MagSafe-like charger, roughly the size of a Tic Tac, works while the glasses are worn.

Apple hasn’t announced a price, battery spec, or final name, and no source gives Gulf availability.
According to Bloomberg, Apple wants its App Store developers to help it compete with market leader Meta and its Ray-Ban glasses.
Samsung has confirmed its own AR glasses for 2026, as Tbreak reported .
The glasses have Wi-Fi, so certain functions outside third-party apps keep working when the iPhone isn’t nearby.
Apple is also stressing sound quality, which employees have called industry-leading, with support for phone calls, music, and FaceTime audio.
Employees reportedly describe the product as “AirPods for your face”; camera-equipped AirPods are a separate product.
According to The Verge , the newly revamped Siri AI, with its fine-grained control over apps, is key to the glasses’ success.
The prototypes, codenamed N50, run a pared-down version of visionOS on a new processor based on Apple’s older smartwatch chips.
A MagSafe-like charger, roughly the size of a Tic Tac, works while the glasses are worn.
MacRumors reported in July that Gurman expects privacy to be a focus.
Gurman reports Apple envisions restaurant reservations through OpenTable, rides through Uber or Lyft, Starbucks orders, Amazon shopping, and Fandango tickets.
Built-in functions cover Visual Intelligence, notifications, messages, calendar, reminders, music, and smart home control.
According to Digital Trends, software is running behind, though the June reveal and year-end shipping are still in place and much of the hardware is largely finalised.

sources.title: Apple’s First Smart Glasses Will Be iPhone-Only, Gurman Reports - AndroidPure
passages: Apple’s first smart glasses will rely on Siri to control apps on a paired iPhone, according to a report from Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman.
The glasses will reportedly need a recent iPhone, and current plans include no Android support.
As of November 16, Apple has not commented on the report.
For Android owners, the iPhone requirement is the key detail.
That leaves Android users with options like Meta’s Ray-Ban line and Google and Samsung’s Android XR glasses, which start at $395 .
Siri’s app-action controls arrived in the first iOS 27.3 beta, per the report.
It fits with earlier reporting that Siri could become an AI agent that acts inside apps for you.
Plans can change before a 2027 launch, so this isn’t a final word on Android compatibility.
Apple is also said to be experimenting with extra privacy features.
Recording indicators matter on camera glasses, as Ray-Ban Meta owners’ reports of unprompted recordings showed earlier.
They stay on the iPhone, and developers would not build separate glasses apps.

extraction.body: Apple’s first smart glasses will rely on Siri to control apps on a paired iPhone, according to a report from Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman. The glasses will reportedly need a recent iPhone, and current plans include no Android support. As of November 16, Apple has not commented on the report. The glasses, code-named N50, are reportedly due to be unveiled at WWDC in June 2027. Shipments would begin before the end of that year. Gurman cautions that the software and AI work is running late, so that timeline could slip. The first model reportedly has no AR display. Instead, Siri would use the built-in cameras to answer questions about what you’re looking at. The report’s examples include identifying a building and suggesting meals from what’s in your fridge. Siri could also give directions and translate signs or conversations. Apps would not run on the glasses themselves. They stay on the iPhone, and developers would not build separate glasses apps. Instead, they would let Siri trigger specific features inside their existing iPhone apps. Think booking a ride, reserving a table, ordering coffee or buying movie tickets. Some of that groundwork is already in place. Siri’s app-action controls arrived in the first iOS 27.3 beta, per the report. Apple’s own apps get support in December, and third-party apps follow in 2027. It fits with earlier reporting that Siri could become an AI agent that acts inside apps for you. Beyond Siri, the glasses would handle calls, messages, notifications, calendars and reminders. Music playback and smart-home controls are on the list too. Employees reportedly rate the audio among the best in the industry. Gurman describes the current prototype as slightly thinner than Meta’s second-generation Ray-Ban glasses. Oval camera openings sit flush in the frame. A light on the front shows when the glasses are in use or charging. Apple is also said to be experimenting with extra privacy features. Recording indicators matter on camera glasses, as Ray-Ban Meta owners’ reports of unprompted recordings showed earlier. Charging uses a flat, three-pin magnetic connector near the end of the left temple arm. The report puts it at roughly the size of a Tic Tac. It’s not yet clear whether that design will make it to the final product. Inside, the prototypes run a reduced version of visionOS 28. The chip is reportedly derived from older Apple Watch processors. Wi-Fi keeps some functions, such as audio, working without an iPhone nearby. Even so, the glasses are not meant to be a standalone device. For Android owners, the iPhone requirement is the key detail. Under current plans, Apple’s glasses won’t pair with Android phones. That leaves Android users with options like Meta’s Ray-Ban line and Google and Samsung’s Android XR glasses, which start at $395 . Plans can change before a 2027 launch, so this isn’t a final word on Android compatibility. The report doesn’t mention pricing. Gurman adds that Apple’s camera-equipped AirPods are still planned for late 2027. Source: Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman, via MacRumors , The Verge

sources.title: 2 Hedge Fund Managers Want Jensen Huang Back. Could He Return as Nvidia CEO? - Yahoo Finance
passages: Now, two prominent hedge fund managers , Brad Gerstner of Altimeter Capital and Gavin Baker of Atreides Management, are calling for the board to consider bringing back Huang.

In a letter to the board, the two investors asked the directors "to pursue a slow, measured, and deliberate process regarding the future of Nvidia that leaves all options on the table, including the potential return of Jensen Huang." They added, "The Founder and longtime incredible leader of this extraordinary company has earned the right for a deliberate process that avoids any needless rush to replace him before all the facts are known."
At this point, Huang's return seems like a long shot and is not a reason to buy the stock.
Bringing him back could lead to further chaos at the company, especially while Nvidia is being investigated by regulators.
Jensen Huang's departure has shocked the business world and left Nvidia (NASDAQ:NVDA) investors wondering what happens next.
Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005.
But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase.
It could take months and multiple investigations to determine if Jensen Huang or Nvidia broke any laws or what, if anything, may have been leaked to Alice Huang.
Jensen Huang speaking on stage. Image source: Getty Images.
At minimum, for Huang to return, there would need to be a full exoneration by the federal government over the chip export ordeal, and that will take time.
Prior to the recent slide, Nvidia had added roughly $5 trillion in market value over the last decade, and its investors don't want to see that continue to erode.

Nvidia announced Huang's resignation Thursday morning after meeting the night before to reportedly oust him, and it's not clear if Huang willingly agreed to walk away in the end, or if he was pushed out.
Shares of the AI chip leader tumbled 15% last week as the drama unfolded around Huang, and are down a third from their peak in October.

Jensen Huang's departure has shocked the business world and left Nvidia (NASDAQ:NVDA) investors wondering what happens next. Shares of the AI chip leader tumbled 15% last week as the drama unfolded around Huang, and are down a third from their peak in October. Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 16x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue » However, over a longer time frame, Nvidia has been one of the greatest engines of wealth creation in human history. Prior to the recent slide, Nvidia had added roughly $5 trillion in market value over the last decade, and its investors don't want to see that continue to erode. Now, two prominent hedge fund managers , Brad Gerstner of Altimeter Capital and Gavin Baker of Atreides Management, are calling for the board to consider bringing back Huang. In a letter to the board, the two investors asked the directors "to pursue a slow, measured, and deliberate process regarding the future of Nvidia that leaves all options on the table, including the potential return of Jensen Huang." They added, "The Founder and longtime incredible leader of this extraordinary company has earned the right for a deliberate process that avoids any needless rush to replace him before all the facts are known." Jensen Huang speaking on stage. Image source: Getty Images. In addition to that letter, an open petition that calls for him to be reinstated has received more than 80,000 signatures, and hundreds of Nvidia employees have signed a letter calling for Huang to be brought back. Clearly, there's a strong interest in his return. This call comes at the same time that the federal government said that it has not determined that Alice Huang, the Megaspeed executive with whom Jensen Huang had an affair, is a spy. In other words, she was not directly employed by Beijing and may instead have been an "asset," someone who could have passed along information to Chinese intelligence. It could take months and multiple investigations to determine if Jensen Huang or Nvidia broke any laws or what, if anything, may have been leaked to Alice Huang. At minimum, for Huang to return, there would need to be a full exoneration by the federal government over the chip export ordeal, and that will take time. Jensen has agreed to testify before Congress. Nvidia announced Huang's resignation Thursday morning after meeting the night before to reportedly oust him, and it's not clear if Huang willingly agreed to walk away in the end, or if he was pushed out. According to Bloomberg , Huang seemed to express remorse before he resigned, saying, "I'm a piece of sh--." The episode has been humiliating for him, and the resignation may have come to avoid more dirty laundry being aired in the media. After the resignation, Reuters reported a third affair with an unnamed employee, and there could be more. In other words, it's unclear if Huang wants his job back right now. At this point, Huang's return seems like a long shot and is not a reason to buy the stock. Bringing him back could lead to further chaos at the company, especially while Nvidia is being investigated by regulators. The calls could grow louder, though, depending on how the company performs without him, and if enough shareholders want him back, they could install a new board to do so. Rather than indulging in that drama, investors are better off focusing on the facts on the ground and what they mean for the future of Nvidia. We'll get more insights when the company reports third-quarter earnings on Tuesday during the earnings call. How CFO and interim CEO Colette Kress handles the call and what information she shares should help signal where the company goes from here. The only thing that's certain for Nvidia is there's plenty of uncertainty ahead. extraction.body: Just three days after the high-profile resignation of the founder of the world's most valuable chipmaker, his supporters in Silicon Valley have set up a dedicated war room to pressure the board of directors. However, regaining the seat will not be easy for the billionaire: he does not hold a controlling stake, while the corporation is already scouting for his replacement and bracing for scrutiny from Washington. Former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, who resigned on Thursday, November 12, following the exposure of extramarital relationships with an alleged Chinese spy and a direct subordinate, is already discussing a plan to return to the company with his confidants. This was reported on Sunday, November 15, by the British newspaper Financial Times. According to an associate of the businessman, Silicon Valley top executives have formed a dedicated "war room" to lobby Nvidia's board of directors for Huang's reinstatement, as well as to try to secure support in the White House. "Everyone who matters in tech outside of the frontier labs loves Jensen," said an interlocutor of the publication, adding that these efforts have the backing of the former CEO himself. Over the weekend, the public campaign for the return of the founder of the $4 trillion corporation gained momentum. An open letter to the board of directors demanding to "Bring Jensen Back" was supported by Tesla and SpaceX chief Elon Musk, Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney, as well as several Nvidia employees. Back on Friday, major shareholders of the company—Altimeter Capital founder Brad Gerstner and Atreides Management head Gavin Baker—published an appeal to the corporate leadership, urging them to keep "all options on the table, including the potential return of Jensen Huang," given his decades of service and the uncertainty surrounding the future of the business. Despite pressure from billionaires and investors, the push to rehabilitate Huang faces severe legal and political obstacles. Unlike many other tech titan founders, Huang does not hold a controlling stake in Nvidia and therefore cannot veto decisions made by the board of directors. The board itself is currently conducting an independent investigation into the former chief's conduct. Even those in the businessman's camp acknowledge the weakness of his position. "An affair with a subordinate is a firing offense," admitted one member of Huang's support group. Aside from the internal workplace affair with Vice President of Healthcare Kimberly Powell, Huang's primary problem stems from his connection to Alice Huang, head of the Singapore-based company Megaspeed, which US authorities suspect of espionage and smuggling chips into China. This episode has drawn intense scrutiny toward how Nvidia monitors the sales of its artificial intelligence processors to clients in Asia. On Sunday, November 15, US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent publicly called for a "radical refresh" in Nvidia's leadership following the departure of its founder. Meanwhile, the corporation's interim CEO Colette Kress is preparing the company for the release of its quarterly financial report on Tuesday, while the board of directors is already looking for a permanent successor. According to the Financial Times, Nvidia representatives have approached Rene Haas, CEO of the British processor architecture designer Arm Holdings, with an offer to head the corporation, though officially the company states that a formal process to select a new leader has not yet been launched. Representatives of Nvidia and Jensen Huang himself declined to comment on his potential return.

coreStoryFacts.text: Now, two prominent hedge fund managers , Brad Gerstner of Altimeter Capital and Gavin Baker of Atreides Management, are calling for the board to consider bringing back Huang.

In a letter to the board, the two investors asked the directors "to pursue a slow, measured, and deliberate process regarding the future of Nvidia that leaves all options on the table, including the potential return of Jensen Huang." They added, "The Founder and longtime incredible leader of this extraordinary company has earned the right for a deliberate process that avoids any needless rush to replace him before all the facts are known."
At this point, Huang's return seems like a long shot and is not a reason to buy the stock.
Bringing him back could lead to further chaos at the company, especially while Nvidia is being investigated by regulators.
Jensen Huang's departure has shocked the business world and left Nvidia (NASDAQ:NVDA) investors wondering what happens next.
Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005.
But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase.
It could take months and multiple investigations to determine if Jensen Huang or Nvidia broke any laws or what, if anything, may have been leaked to Alice Huang.
Jensen Huang speaking on stage. Image source: Getty Images.
At minimum, for Huang to return, there would need to be a full exoneration by the federal government over the chip export ordeal, and that will take time.
Prior to the recent slide, Nvidia had added roughly $5 trillion in market value over the last decade, and its investors don't want to see that continue to erode.

Nvidia announced Huang's resignation Thursday morning after meeting the night before to reportedly oust him, and it's not clear if Huang willingly agreed to walk away in the end, or if he was pushed out.

extraction.body: Just three days after the high-profile resignation of the founder of the world's most valuable chipmaker, his supporters in Silicon Valley have set up a dedicated war room to pressure the board of directors. However, regaining the seat will not be easy for the billionaire: he does not hold a controlling stake, while the corporation is already scouting for his replacement and bracing for scrutiny from Washington. Former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, who resigned on Thursday, November 12, following the exposure of extramarital relationships with an alleged Chinese spy and a direct subordinate, is already discussing a plan to return to the company with his confidants. This was reported on Sunday, November 15, by the British newspaper Financial Times. According to an associate of the businessman, Silicon Valley top executives have formed a dedicated "war room" to lobby Nvidia's board of directors for Huang's reinstatement, as well as to try to secure support in the White House. "Everyone who matters in tech outside of the frontier labs loves Jensen," said an interlocutor of the publication, adding that these efforts have the backing of the former CEO himself. Over the weekend, the public campaign for the return of the founder of the $4 trillion corporation gained momentum. An open letter to the board of directors demanding to "Bring Jensen Back" was supported by Tesla and SpaceX chief Elon Musk, Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney, as well as several Nvidia employees. Back on Friday, major shareholders of the company—Altimeter Capital founder Brad Gerstner and Atreides Management head Gavin Baker—published an appeal to the corporate leadership, urging them to keep "all options on the table, including the potential return of Jensen Huang," given his decades of service and the uncertainty surrounding the future of the business. Despite pressure from billionaires and investors, the push to rehabilitate Huang faces severe legal and political obstacles. Unlike many other tech titan founders, Huang does not hold a controlling stake in Nvidia and therefore cannot veto decisions made by the board of directors. The board itself is currently conducting an independent investigation into the former chief's conduct. Even those in the businessman's camp acknowledge the weakness of his position. "An affair with a subordinate is a firing offense," admitted one member of Huang's support group. Aside from the internal workplace affair with Vice President of Healthcare Kimberly Powell, Huang's primary problem stems from his connection to Alice Huang, head of the Singapore-based company Megaspeed, which US authorities suspect of espionage and smuggling chips into China. This episode has drawn intense scrutiny toward how Nvidia monitors the sales of its artificial intelligence processors to clients in Asia. On Sunday, November 15, US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent publicly called for a "radical refresh" in Nvidia's leadership following the departure of its founder. Meanwhile, the corporation's interim CEO Colette Kress is preparing the company for the release of its quarterly financial report on Tuesday, while the board of directors is already looking for a permanent successor. According to the Financial Times, Nvidia representatives have approached Rene Haas, CEO of the British processor architecture designer Arm Holdings, with an offer to head the corporation, though officially the company states that a formal process to select a new leader has not yet been launched. Representatives of Nvidia and Jensen Huang himself declined to comment on his potential return.

Huang, 63, stepped down on Thursday from the top role at the $4 trillion tech giant he co-founded after it was revealed that he may have also had a second affair with Nvidia's Vice President of Healthcare Kimberly Powell. Hours later, Reuters reported that the former CEO had yet another, third extramarital relationship with another unidentified Nvidia employee. Huang has only admitted to the affair with the alleged spy, Alice Huang, whom he is not related to. Despite the seriousness and recency of the philandering accusations, Huang has already been holding discussions with powerful Silicon Valley figures about returning as CEO, sources involved in the effort told the Financial Times . An ally of the ex-CEO told the publication that Silicon Valley executives have been putting together a 'war room' to lobby for Huang's return to Nvidia. The executives are hoping to gain backing from the White House , and their efforts are being supported by Huang behind the scenes, the source said. Many investors, Nvidia employees and Silicon Valley executives have also already publicly supported Huang, citing his enormously successful 33-year leadership of the company and vision that placed the business at the heart of the AI boom. An open letter calling for Huang's return has been supported by Elon Musk and Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney, as well as nearly 9,000 former and current Nvidia employees and more than 83,000 investors. President Trump has maintained a positive tone about Huang since the affairs were reported and the ex-CEO stepped down, calling him 'a tremendous talent.' Trump also said, however, that Huang was right to resign if it is confirmed that Alice was a spy. 'It's sad. He’s a tremendous talent. He did something nobody else did. He has a chip that’s so complex, so brilliant, you can’t copy it. What he’s done is incredible, he built an incredible company,' Trump told CNN's Stephen A Smith on Thursday. Smith asked Trump point blank if Huang was right to step down, which led to a rare pause from Trump before answering. 'The big thing was, was the woman a spy? Huang did not have a controlling share of Nvidia in contrast to many other Silicon Valley executives, which made him unable to override any board decision. sources.title: COP31 launches new priorities for AI firms to provide reliable information on climate change - Peoples Gazette Nigeria
passages: The United Nations has launched new global priorities at COP31 to ensure that artificial intelligence (AI) provides reliable information on climate change and promotes transparency about its environmental impact.
They require AI companies to assess how their systems affect climate information integrity and publish the findings.
Governments are expected to integrate information integrity into their national AI strategies and climate plans.

Beyond the use of AI, the initiative also seeks to address the role of digital advertising in spreading climate disinformation as the advertising supply chain lacks transparency, making it difficult for brands to know who and what their money funds, including climate disinformation.

The United Nations has launched new global priorities at COP31 to ensure that artificial intelligence (AI) provides reliable information on climate change and promotes transparency about its environmental impact. The Independent International Scientific Panel on AI warned that producing fluent text is easier than producing factual information. It noted that the risks could heighten during climate disasters, when AI-generated images and videos spread faster than official warnings. In response to the concerns, the priorities put forward by the Global Initiative’s co-chairs Brazil, the UN and UNESCO, are based on transparency, accountability and human rights. They require AI companies to assess how their systems affect climate information integrity and publish the findings. They also require the companies to disclose their energy use and carbon, water and land footprints. Governments are expected to integrate information integrity into their national AI strategies and climate plans. Beyond the use of AI, the initiative also seeks to address the role of digital advertising in spreading climate disinformation as the advertising supply chain lacks transparency, making it difficult for brands to know who and what their money funds, including climate disinformation. The Charter for Climate Information Integrity in Advertising, launched by the Conscious Advertising Network (CAN) and Climate Action Against Disinformation (CAAD), with support from the Global Initiative, proposes four major measures. These include transparency across the advertising supply chain, verification of all advertisers on digital platforms, action against greenwashing and public disclosure of advertising actors’ relationships with fossil fuel companies. Germany committed €2 million to the Global Fund for Information Integrity on Climate Change, administered by UNESCO, to support research, develop communication strategies and undertake public awareness campaigns. The initiative urged other countries to invest in the fund. Since the information integrity entered a COP outcome decision at COP30 in Belém, 29 countries and the European Union have signed up to it and begun implementing its provisions. The Belém Declaration on Information Integrity on Climate Change remains open to further endorsements. Governments are expected to integrate information integrity into their national AI strategies and climate plans.

Beyond the use of AI, the initiative also seeks to address the role of digital advertising in spreading climate disinformation as the advertising supply chain lacks transparency, making it difficult for brands to know who and what their money funds, including climate disinformation.

The priorities, put forward by Global Initiative co-chairs Brazil, the UN and UNESCO, target two sides of one AI information gap: the reliability of the climate information people receive from AI, and the reliability of information about AI’s own impact on the climate. More and more people are turning to AI for climate information, yet the Independent International Scientific Panel on AI warns that “producing fluent text is easier than producing factual text”. The risks can heighten during climate disasters, when AI-generated images and videos can spread faster than oﬃcial warnings. Meanwhile, the public is asked to accept claims about AI’s own climate impact without the necessary data to judge. Building on the Belém Declaration and the UN Global Principles for Information Integrity, the Priorities rest on transparency, accountability and human rights. For AI companies, this means assessing how their systems affect climate information integrity and publishing the findings, and disclosing their energy use and carbon, water and land footprints. Actions for states include integrating information integrity into national AI strategies and climate plans. Global Advertising Charter says: follow the money. Advertising is the dominant business model of the digital information ecosystem. Yet because the advertising supply chain is opaque, brands often cannot tell who and what their money funds, including climate disinformation. To change that, the Charter for Climate Information Integrity in Advertising, launched by Conscious Advertising Network (CAN) and Climate Action Against Disinformation (CAAD) and supported by the Global Initiative, calls for transparency across the advertising supply chain to ensure advertisers have visibility of advertising placement while respecting user privacy. The charter also calls for verification of all advertisers on digital platforms, action on greenwashing and ensuring advertising actors publicly disclose their relationships with fossil fuel actors. Strengthening information integrity requires resources. At COP31, the Global Initiative called for new investment in the information people rely on to understand and act on climate change. Germany answered the call, committing EUR 2 million to the Global Fund for Information Integrity on Climate Change, administered by UNESCO, for grants to support research, develop communication strategies and undertake public awareness campaigns. The Initiative urged other countries to invest in the Fund. Political momentum grows. One year after information integrity entered a COP (Conference of the Parties) outcome decision for the first time, at COP30 in Belém, 29 countries and the European Union have now signed and are implementing the Belém Declaration on Information Integrity on Climate Change, which remains open for endorsement. extraction.body: A business news platform with a sustainable focus. Featuring the latest sustainability news and ESG insight, viewed through a business lens. A new initiative to ensure the reliability of climate information generated by artificial intelligence is being launched by the Global Initiative for Information Integrity on Climate Change. The Priorities for Action on AI and Climate Information Integrity, which is set to be launched at COP31 on 13 November, follows on from a warning by the Independent International Scientific Panel on AI that as more people turn to chatbots for climate information, ‘producing fluent text is easier than producing factual text’. The priorities will seek to set out measures that governments, AI actors, advertisers, researchers, journalists and other related parties can do to ensure climate information on AI is trustworthy. A separate initiative, the Charter for Climate Information Integrity in Advertising , will be launched on 14 November, which calls on advertisers, advertising agencies and digital platforms to stop funding climate disinformation. Both initiatives follow on from progress made at COP30, where information integrity entered a COP outcome decision for the first time – the Belém Declaration on Information Integrity on Climate Change. To date, 29 countries, along with the European Union, have committed to the declaration. The Global Initiative will also hold two pavilion sessions on the topic – on 14 November, the SDG Pavilion will host a discussion on the relationship between climate information integrity and delivery of the Sustainable Development Goals, subtitled ‘From Words To Action’. This will be followed by a session at the UN Pavilion on 16 November, which will examine what effective policy looks like in practice. The Global Initiative for Information Integrity on Climate Change was launched by the Government of Brazil, the United Nations and UNESCO at the G20 Leaders’ Summit in Rio de Janeiro, which took place in November 2024. It brings together governments, international organisations and civil society to strengthen research and action on climate information integrity. The Global Fund for Information Integrity on Climate Change also falls under its remit. Read more here .

(AP Photo/Tatan Syuflana, File) ANTALYA – As world leaders gathered for United Nations climate talks in the Turkish resort town of Antalya on Wednesday, host Turkey urged countries to commit to a zero-waste initiative aimed at reducing emissions and helping get global efforts to curb climate change back on track. Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan touted his country's progress on recycling, saying its rate had risen from about 13% in 2017, when the zero waste movement began, to about 40% by the end of 2025. "Some 90 million tons of waste have been brought back into our economy,” Erdogan told the leaders' summit. “We’ll not stop here and we will continue working and making every effort until we achieve the goal of zero waste." Turkey has outlined 10 priorities for this year’s climate talks, known as COP31 , with a pledge to accelerate electrification and the zero-waste initiatives emerging as major talking points during the opening days of the conference. Turkish first lady Emine Erdogan, who attended Wednesday's talks, has been a driving force behind the zero-waste initiative, which aims to reduce methane emissions, cut food waste and promote a circular economy in which materials are reused and recycled. “Recovered materials can be cheaper when reliable supplies, efficient processing and nearby demand outweigh the costs of collection, sorting and transport,” said Samed Agirbas, president of the nonprofit Zero Waste Foundation and a COP31 high-level climate champion. If implemented, energy experts say the initiatives could slow global warming and reduce the environmental footprint of renewable energy technologies, like solar panels and batteries. But there is still a risk these climate ambitions may fall flat. Conference agreements are often nonbinding and past hosts have been criticized for failing to follow through on promises. Turkey also faces scrutiny over its own climate record. “The Zero Waste target is a good target. It definitely needs to be supported with concrete measures and further action,” said Berk Butan, who heads the waste campaign for Greenpeace Turkey. “But fundamentally, we also need to recognize its shortcomings.” As the second biggest cause of climate change after carbon dioxide, the reduction of methane emissions could significantly slow global warming, according to the U.N. During the first three days of the climate talks, leaders repeatedly called for urgent climate action. The U.N. recently had to readjust a decades-old goal of limiting the rise of global temperatures because the world was blowing past previous thresholds. While Turkey wants countries to commit to reducing methane emissions, it has not signed the Global Methane Pledge. Launched at the 2021 climate talks in Glasgow, the initiative aims to reduce methane emissions by at least 30% from 2020 levels by 2030. Turkey is also the world’s fifth-biggest emitter of methane from solid waste, according to nonprofit emissions tracker Climate TRACE. “Methane emissions from waste disposal are an important challenge,” said Agirbas, with the Zero Waste Foundation. Circular economy may dent emissions, but challenges remain A circular economy — an economic model that generally prioritizes recycling and other regenerative approaches that create less waste— would help reduce emissions, but not every country has the resources to take such steps. Ke Wang, an energy expert at the WRI's Polsky Center for the Global Energy Transition, said that this is “a vital strategy for cutting greenhouse gas emissions." But recycling food waste is difficult because it decomposes quickly, making separation and processing expensive. Collecting and transporting wet, smelly food waste also requires specialized logistics and infrastructure that many countries lack. “Waste and food loss account for almost 10% of total emissions, so we need to integrate these actions,” Adalberto Maluf, a top official in Brazil’s environment ministry, told The Associated Press. The recycling of already-mined materials is key to reducing the reliance on mining, according to experts, which will only become more important as the world relies more on critical mineral-dependent renewable technologies. The International Energy Agency estimates that scaling up recycling could lower the need for new mining by between 25% and 40% by 2050. Most countries don’t recycle critical materials because it’s cheaper to mine them. The technology and infrastructure needed to recycle these materials are also concentrated in a handful of nations, like China. The European Union and the U.S. will likely only have the capacity to recycle 30% of their raw materials by 2040, according to the IEA. “We must do a better job with our materials retrieval, reuse and recycling,” said Aimee Boulanger, executive director of the Initiative for Responsible Mining Assurance. She stressed the need to create incentives for “retrieving the materials, taking things apart, being able to reuse them again in a circular way.” Arasu reported from Bengaluru, India, Milko from Islamabad, Pakistan and Delgado from Bangkok. ANTALYA – As world leaders gathered for United Nations climate talks in the Turkish resort town of Antalya on Wednesday, host Turkey urged countries to commit to a zero-waste initiative aimed at reducing emissions and helping get global efforts to curb climate change back on track.

Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan touted his country's progress on recycling, saying its rate had risen from about 13% in 2017, when the zero waste movement began, to about 40% by the end of 2025.

"Some 90 million tons of waste have been brought back into our economy,” Erdogan told the leaders' summit. “We’ll not stop here and we will continue working and making every effort until we achieve the goal of zero waste."

Turkey has outlined 10 priorities for this year’s climate talks, known as COP31 , with a pledge to accelerate electrification and the zero-waste initiatives emerging as major talking points during the opening days of the conference.

Turkish first lady Emine Erdogan, who attended Wednesday's talks, has been a driving force behind the zero-waste initiative, which aims to reduce methane emissions, cut food waste and promote a circular economy in which materials are reused and recycled.

“Recovered materials can be cheaper when reliable supplies, efficient processing and nearby demand outweigh the costs of collection, sorting and transport,” said Samed Agirbas, president of the nonprofit Zero Waste Foundation and a COP31 high-level climate champion.

If implemented, energy experts say the initiatives could slow global warming and reduce the environmental footprint of renewable energy technologies, like solar panels and batteries. But there is still a risk these climate ambitions may fall flat.
Conference agreements are often nonbinding and past hosts have been criticized for failing to follow through on promises. Turkey also faces scrutiny over its own climate record.

“The Zero Waste target is a good target. It definitely needs to be supported with concrete measures and further action,” said Berk Butan, who heads the waste campaign for Greenpeace Turkey. “But fundamentally, we also need to recognize its shortcomings.”

As the second biggest cause of climate change after carbon dioxide, the reduction of methane emissions could significantly slow global warming, according to the U.N. During the first three days of the climate talks, leaders repeatedly called for urgent climate action.
The U.N. recently had to readjust a decades-old goal of limiting the rise of global temperatures because the world was blowing past previous thresholds.

While Turkey wants countries to commit to reducing methane emissions, it has not signed the Global Methane Pledge. Launched at the 2021 climate talks in Glasgow, the initiative aims to reduce methane emissions by at least 30% from 2020 levels by 2030.
Turkey is also the world’s fifth-biggest emitter of methane from solid waste, according to nonprofit emissions tracker Climate TRACE.
“Methane emissions from waste disposal are an important challenge,” said Agirbas, with the Zero Waste Foundation.
Circular economy may dent emissions, but challenges remain

A circular economy — an economic model that generally prioritizes recycling and other regenerative approaches that create less waste— would help reduce emissions, but not every country has the resources to take such steps.
Ke Wang, an energy expert at the WRI's Polsky Center for the Global Energy Transition, said that this is “a vital strategy for cutting greenhouse gas emissions."

But recycling food waste is difficult because it decomposes quickly, making separation and processing expensive. Collecting and transporting wet, smelly food waste also requires specialized logistics and infrastructure that many countries lack.
“Waste and food loss account for almost 10% of total emissions, so we need to integrate these actions,” Adalberto Maluf, a top official in Brazil’s environment ministry, told The Associated Press.

The recycling of already-mined materials is key to reducing the reliance on mining, according to experts, which will only become more important as the world relies more on critical mineral-dependent renewable technologies.
The International Energy Agency estimates that scaling up recycling could lower the need for new mining by between 25% and 40% by 2050.

Most countries don’t recycle critical materials because it’s cheaper to mine them. The technology and infrastructure needed to recycle these materials are also concentrated in a handful of nations, like China. The European Union and the U.S. will likely only have the capacity to recycle 30% of their raw materials by 2040, according to the IEA.

“We must do a better job with our materials retrieval, reuse and recycling,” said Aimee Boulanger, executive director of the Initiative for Responsible Mining Assurance. She stressed the need to create incentives for “retrieving the materials, taking things apart, being able to reuse them again in a circular way.”
Arasu reported from Bengaluru, India, Milko from Islamabad, Pakistan and Delgado from Bangkok.

Antalya, Nov 13 (SocialNews.XYZ) At COP31, the Global Initiative for Information Integrity on Climate Change on Friday launched the Priorities for Action on AI for Climate Information Integrity, setting out what states, AI actors, advertisers, researchers, journalists and funders can do so that people can rely on climate information from AI, and about it.

The priorities, put forward by Global Initiative co-chairs Brazil, the UN and UNESCO, target two sides of one AI information gap: the reliability of the climate information people receive from AI, and the reliability of information about AI’s own impact on the climate.
More and more people are turning to AI for climate information, yet the Independent International Scientific Panel on AI warns that “producing fluent text is easier than producing factual text”.
The risks can heighten during climate disasters, when AI-generated images and videos can spread faster than oﬃcial warnings.

Meanwhile, the public is asked to accept claims about AI’s own climate impact without the necessary data to judge. Building on the Belém Declaration and the UN Global Principles for Information Integrity, the Priorities rest on transparency, accountability and human rights.
For AI companies, this means assessing how their systems affect climate information integrity and publishing the findings, and disclosing their energy use and carbon, water and land footprints.
Actions for states include integrating information integrity into national AI strategies and climate plans.

Global Advertising Charter says: follow the money. Advertising is the dominant business model of the digital information ecosystem. Yet because the advertising supply chain is opaque, brands often cannot tell who and what their money funds, including climate disinformation.

To change that, the Charter for Climate Information Integrity in Advertising, launched by Conscious Advertising Network (CAN) and Climate Action Against Disinformation (CAAD) and supported by the Global Initiative, calls for transparency across the advertising supply chain to ensure advertisers have visibility of advertising placement while respecting user privacy.

The charter also calls for verification of all advertisers on digital platforms, action on greenwashing and ensuring advertising actors publicly disclose their relationships with fossil fuel actors. Strengthening information integrity requires resources.

passages: The marks attained by the top scorer ⁠on South Korea’s national exam for aspiring tax accountants this year seemed too good to be true.
On Sunday, sceptics were ⁠proven right when he ⁠confessed to ​using generative AI to cheat.
His score of 397.5 out of 400 points in the first round, with only one wrong answer out of 160 questions, had sparked accusations that he cheated using smart glasses, which he initially denied.
The scandal has followed months of speculation after he scored near-perfect marks on hundreds of questions over two exams ⁠taken in April and July.
He said he had cheated by ‌taking photos of the exam questions with a microcamera, sending them to an AI tool and checking the answers on a smartphone.

It comes just days before Thursday’s annual national college entrance exam, ‌a high-pressure event for which many South ​Korean students will have spent much of their lives preparing.

extraction.body: South Korean Police Investigate Top Tax Accountant Exam Candidate for AI Cheating South Korean authorities have launched an investigation after the top scorer in a national tax accountant exam confessed to using artificial intelligence to cheat. The candidate, who ranked first in both rounds of the qualification exam, admitted via his lawyer that he photographed questions with a miniature camera, sent them to AI for answers, and viewed the results on his smartphone. This case adds to growing concerns about high-tech cheating methods, following recent incidents involving smart glasses in other certifications and upcoming plans to address similar issues in the national university entrance exam. South Korean police said Sunday they had launched an investigation after the top scorer in a national tax accountant exam admitted to using artificial intelligence to cheat. The candidate, who ranked first in both rounds of the qualification exam held in April and July, confessed through his lawyer that he used AI to obtain answers during the tests. His score of 397.5 out of 400 points in the first round, with only one wrong answer out of 160 questions, had sparked accusations that he cheated using smart glasses, which he initially denied.“We received a written confession through the test taker’s lawyer this morning regarding cheating on the tax accountant exam,” the Seoul Metropolitan Police Agency said, adding the case had been assigned to investigators. In a video posted on his lawyer’s YouTube channel, the candidate said he “deeply regretted” what he had done.“I used a miniature camera to photograph the exam questions and sent them to AI, then checked the answers on my smartphone,” he said. “I wanted to make money, and I hated seeing myself disappointing my parents after quitting a good job,” he said. The examination is administered by the Human Resources Development Service of Korea , which said two supervisors were present when the candidate sat the test.The HRDK said Sunday an “AI inspector” caught a test taker wearing smart glasses during a gas engineer certification exam last month. In October, the government announced plans to file criminal complaints against students caught using such devices in the national university entrance exam. With the annual college entrance test, known as the “Suneung”, due to take place on November 19, the presidential office said it was treating the issue seriously.The presidential office “has been working hard to come up with measures to address it,” chief of staff Lim Kwang-hyun told reporters.“A meeting to discuss those measures will be held this afternoon, chaired by the presidential chief of staff for policy, and preparations are underway,” he added.

The scandal has followed months of speculation after he scored near-perfect marks on hundreds of questions over two exams ⁠taken in April and July.
He said he had cheated by ‌taking photos of the exam questions with a microcamera, sending them to an AI tool and checking the answers on a smartphone.

It comes just days before Thursday’s annual national college entrance exam, ‌a high-pressure event for which many South ​Korean students will have spent much of their lives preparing.

extraction.body: South Korean Police Investigate Top Tax Accountant Exam Candidate for AI Cheating South Korean authorities have launched an investigation after the top scorer in a national tax accountant exam confessed to using artificial intelligence to cheat. The candidate, who ranked first in both rounds of the qualification exam, admitted via his lawyer that he photographed questions with a miniature camera, sent them to AI for answers, and viewed the results on his smartphone. This case adds to growing concerns about high-tech cheating methods, following recent incidents involving smart glasses in other certifications and upcoming plans to address similar issues in the national university entrance exam. South Korean police said Sunday they had launched an investigation after the top scorer in a national tax accountant exam admitted to using artificial intelligence to cheat. The candidate, who ranked first in both rounds of the qualification exam held in April and July, confessed through his lawyer that he used AI to obtain answers during the tests. His score of 397.5 out of 400 points in the first round, with only one wrong answer out of 160 questions, had sparked accusations that he cheated using smart glasses, which he initially denied.“We received a written confession through the test taker’s lawyer this morning regarding cheating on the tax accountant exam,” the Seoul Metropolitan Police Agency said, adding the case had been assigned to investigators. In a video posted on his lawyer’s YouTube channel, the candidate said he “deeply regretted” what he had done.“I used a miniature camera to photograph the exam questions and sent them to AI, then checked the answers on my smartphone,” he said. “I wanted to make money, and I hated seeing myself disappointing my parents after quitting a good job,” he said. The examination is administered by the Human Resources Development Service of Korea , which said two supervisors were present when the candidate sat the test.The HRDK said Sunday an “AI inspector” caught a test taker wearing smart glasses during a gas engineer certification exam last month. In October, the government announced plans to file criminal complaints against students caught using such devices in the national university entrance exam. With the annual college entrance test, known as the “Suneung”, due to take place on November 19, the presidential office said it was treating the issue seriously.The presidential office “has been working hard to come up with measures to address it,” chief of staff Lim Kwang-hyun told reporters.“A meeting to discuss those measures will be held this afternoon, chaired by the presidential chief of staff for policy, and preparations are underway,” he added.

extraction.body: For more on Jensen Huang’s resignation and the fallout from Nvidia’s leadership crisis, follow Terrence O’Brien. How it started On October 29th, The New York Times reported that Nvidia co-founder and showman CEO Jensen Huang appeared to be the target of a Chinese spy plot. Any major tech CEO potentially being compromised by the Chinese government is concerning — especially Jensen Huang. “If you could draw the network diagram of the entire US AI ecosystem, Nvidia would be at the center of that,” Kyle Chan, a foreign policy fellow at the Brookings Institution’s John L. “If you could draw the diagram of the entire Nvidia ecosystem, a single man is standing at the heart of all of that.” The Times reported that Jensen Huang had developed a “close relationship” with Alice Huang (no relation), an executive at Singapore-based data center company Megaspeed. Alice Huang had been on the American government’s radar for some time, perhaps as early as 2024. Her company was investigated by the US Commerce Department over suspicions it was illegally smuggling Nvidia’s AI chips into China in violation of US government trade restrictions. Singapore authorities confiscated her passport back in June of 2025, eventually barring her from the country, after she reportedly gave “inaccurate information” to police. And perhaps more concerningly, some US officials believed she was passing information, possibly about Nvidia’s designs or the White House’s deliberations over trade restrictions, directly back to Beijing. This made her relationship with Jensen Huang concerning for multiple reasons. Nvidia’s chips are considered crucial to America’s AI superiority and a matter of national security by the White House. The government has restricted the sale of Nvidia’s most advanced chips to China since the Biden administration. But Jensen Huang has routinely pushed to loosen those trade restrictions. On Friday, November 6th, the Times reported that Alice Huang was specifically recruited by China’s Ministry of State Security to spy on Nvidia’s CEO. Though, there is some disagreement among US intelligence officials over the strength of evidence tying Alice Huang to Beijing. While the paper did not confirm it at the time, rumors suggested the “close relationship” between Jensen Huang and Alice Huang was romantic in nature. On Sunday, November 8th, Jensen Huang admitted to having an extramarital affair, but did not name the Megaspeed exec and alleged Chinese spy specifically. Nvidia’s board announced that it was launching an investigation into its CEO shortly after. Many believed that Jensen Huang would survive the scandal. His company’s importance to America’s booming AI industry and his crucial role at the company seemed to make him nearly untouchable. He was, after all, the only CEO the company had ever known with no clear and obvious succession plan in place, and he sat atop an unusual corporate structure with around 60 direct reports. (These numbers are slightly outdated, but according to the Harvard Business Review, 10 to 20 is far more common among Fortune 500 companies, and Tim Cook reportedly had 17 in 2015, which was deemed “a lot” by Business Insider.) Then on Wednesday, November 11th, The New York Times reported that Jensen Huang had a second affair — this one with one of his direct reports, Kimberly Powell, Nvidia’s vice president of health care. Whether that was the last straw or if they were afraid it would be merely the tip of the iceberg, the board was ready to push Jensen Huang out, according to reports circulating that evening. According to Bloomberg, he had accepted his fate Wednesday evening reportedly looking “broken and shattered” and telling people, “I’m a piece of shit.” On Thursday, November 12th, Nvidia announced that Jensen Huang had resigned as CEO of Nvidia. How it’s going CFO Colette Kress was immediately named interim CEO, and acknowledged to employees that this has been an “extraordinarily difficult period.” Harvey Jones was also named the first board chair in the company’s history, already signaling there would be some changes to the corporate structure. In a memo to employees, Jones said the company would “search for a permanent successor looking at both internal and external candidates.” But the destabilizing impact was immediate. Nvidia’s stock closed at an all-time high of $239.24 on October 6th. It’s hard to overstate the importance of Nvidia to the US’s AI arms race with China, and the industry in general. The company has invested $99 billion in various AI labs, startups, and neo clouds. Plus has announced plans to mobilize over $500 billion in financing for building out AI data centers and other infrastructure. Even before Jensen Huang had resigned, Nvidia was already facing a shareholder lawsuit claiming the company had deceived investors. Jensen Huang and the company’s spokespeople insisted that the relationship with Alice Huang and Megaspeed was “completely normal and not unusual.” Only days later, Jensen Huang admitted to an extramarital affair that raised “national security concerns” without naming anyone specifically. According to Reuters, Jensen Huang misled several Nvidia leaders, “including general counsel Tim Teter and chief marketing officer Alison Wagonfeld” about the nature of his relationship with Alice Huang. Many in the AI industry and Silicon Valley jumped to Jensen Huang’s defense. Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney called it a “sad day for NVIDIA, developers, America, and all humanity,” in a particularly hyperbolic post. Elon Musk said on X that it would “be an honor” to hire Jensen Huang. Many of Nvidia’s employees even voiced their support to “bring back THE boss,” on an internal post.

extraction.body: For more on Jensen Huang’s resignation and the fallout from Nvidia’s leadership crisis, follow Terrence O’Brien. How it started On October 29th, The New York Times reported that Nvidia co-founder and showman CEO Jensen Huang appeared to be the target of a Chinese spy plot. Any major tech CEO potentially being compromised by the Chinese government is concerning — especially Jensen Huang. “If you could draw the network diagram of the entire US AI ecosystem, Nvidia would be at the center of that,” Kyle Chan, a foreign policy fellow at the Brookings Institution’s John L. “If you could draw the diagram of the entire Nvidia ecosystem, a single man is standing at the heart of all of that.” The Times reported that Jensen Huang had developed a “close relationship” with Alice Huang (no relation), an executive at Singapore-based data center company Megaspeed. Alice Huang had been on the American government’s radar for some time, perhaps as early as 2024. Her company was investigated by the US Commerce Department over suspicions it was illegally smuggling Nvidia’s AI chips into China in violation of US government trade restrictions. Singapore authorities confiscated her passport back in June of 2025, eventually barring her from the country, after she reportedly gave “inaccurate information” to police. And perhaps more concerningly, some US officials believed she was passing information, possibly about Nvidia’s designs or the White House’s deliberations over trade restrictions, directly back to Beijing. This made her relationship with Jensen Huang concerning for multiple reasons. Nvidia’s chips are considered crucial to America’s AI superiority and a matter of national security by the White House. The government has restricted the sale of Nvidia’s most advanced chips to China since the Biden administration. But Jensen Huang has routinely pushed to loosen those trade restrictions. On Friday, November 6th, the Times reported that Alice Huang was specifically recruited by China’s Ministry of State Security to spy on Nvidia’s CEO. Though, there is some disagreement among US intelligence officials over the strength of evidence tying Alice Huang to Beijing. While the paper did not confirm it at the time, rumors suggested the “close relationship” between Jensen Huang and Alice Huang was romantic in nature. On Sunday, November 8th, Jensen Huang admitted to having an extramarital affair, but did not name the Megaspeed exec and alleged Chinese spy specifically. Nvidia’s board announced that it was launching an investigation into its CEO shortly after. Many believed that Jensen Huang would survive the scandal. His company’s importance to America’s booming AI industry and his crucial role at the company seemed to make him nearly untouchable. He was, after all, the only CEO the company had ever known with no clear and obvious succession plan in place, and he sat atop an unusual corporate structure with around 60 direct reports. (These numbers are slightly outdated, but according to the Harvard Business Review, 10 to 20 is far more common among Fortune 500 companies, and Tim Cook reportedly had 17 in 2015, which was deemed “a lot” by Business Insider.) Then on Wednesday, November 11th, The New York Times reported that Jensen Huang had a second affair — this one with one of his direct reports, Kimberly Powell, Nvidia’s vice president of health care. Whether that was the last straw or if they were afraid it would be merely the tip of the iceberg, the board was ready to push Jensen Huang out, according to reports circulating that evening. According to Bloomberg, he had accepted his fate Wednesday evening reportedly looking “broken and shattered” and telling people, “I’m a piece of shit.” On Thursday, November 12th, Nvidia announced that Jensen Huang had resigned as CEO of Nvidia. How it’s going CFO Colette Kress was immediately named interim CEO, and acknowledged to employees that this has been an “extraordinarily difficult period.” Harvey Jones was also named the first board chair in the company’s history, already signaling there would be some changes to the corporate structure. In a memo to employees, Jones said the company would “search for a permanent successor looking at both internal and external candidates.” But the destabilizing impact was immediate. Nvidia’s stock closed at an all-time high of $239.24 on October 6th. It’s hard to overstate the importance of Nvidia to the US’s AI arms race with China, and the industry in general. The company has invested $99 billion in various AI labs, startups, and neo clouds. Plus has announced plans to mobilize over $500 billion in financing for building out AI data centers and other infrastructure. Even before Jensen Huang had resigned, Nvidia was already facing a shareholder lawsuit claiming the company had deceived investors. Jensen Huang and the company’s spokespeople insisted that the relationship with Alice Huang and Megaspeed was “completely normal and not unusual.” Only days later, Jensen Huang admitted to an extramarital affair that raised “national security concerns” without naming anyone specifically. According to Reuters, Jensen Huang misled several Nvidia leaders, “including general counsel Tim Teter and chief marketing officer Alison Wagonfeld” about the nature of his relationship with Alice Huang. Many in the AI industry and Silicon Valley jumped to Jensen Huang’s defense. Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney called it a “sad day for NVIDIA, developers, America, and all humanity,” in a particularly hyperbolic post. Elon Musk said on X that it would “be an honor” to hire Jensen Huang. Many of Nvidia’s employees even voiced their support to “bring back THE boss,” on an internal post.

The past few months haven't been pretty for semiconductor stocks, as evidenced by the 12% decline in the PHLX Semiconductor Sector index over the past three months. Even Advanced Micro Devices (NASDAQ:AMD) has been caught up in this vortex, experiencing significant volatility amid concerns about the sustainability of artificial intelligence (AI) infrastructure spending, which has been key to the growth of the semiconductor sector. However, the recent weakness in the semiconductor sector has opened up a great opportunity for investors to buy a top stock at an attractive valuation. AMD is emerging as one of the most important players in the AI chip ecosystem, and I won't be surprised to see it embark on a stunning long-term rally. Missed AI’s "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 15x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we’re only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue » Let's see why I think that AMD could be one of the best AI stocks you can buy right now. AMD's Epyc server central processing units (CPUs) are in tremendous demand from hyperscalers and AI companies. As a result, the company's data center revenue jumped by 97% year over year in Q3 to $8.5 billion. The good news for AMD investors is that its data center segment has incredible room for growth. Alphabet 's (NASDAQ:GOOG) (NASDAQ:GOOGL) Google Cloud division has expanded its partnership with AMD to deploy the latter's 5th-generation Epyc server CPUs, security fabric, and x86 software to power its cloud Tensor Processing Unit (TPU) systems. AMD Epyc will serve as the foundation for Google's TPUs, allowing users to run inference applications. The good news for AMD investors is that Alphabet is poised to spend aggressively on its cloud computing infrastructure. After all, the Google Cloud business reported a backlog of a whopping $561 billion at the end of the third quarter. The tech giant expects to recognize half of that backlog in the next two years, which explains why its capital expenditure is ballooning . AMD, therefore, is going to be a direct beneficiary of Alphabet's enormous spending. Not surprisingly, the company expects its growth to accelerate at a solid clip. AMD expects revenue to increase by more than 80% in 2027, fueled by healthy growth in the data center business, where it sees the server CPU total addressable market (TAM) jump to $220 billion by 2030. Importantly, AMD is well-positioned to capitalize on this massive opportunity. It has partnerships with major hyperscalers and AI companies, including OpenAI, Anthropic , Meta Platforms , Microsoft , and others, in the data center segment. These customers should ensure solid long-term revenue growth for AMD, which is precisely what analysts are expecting. AMD Revenue Estimates for Current Fiscal Year data by YCharts The $52.2 billion revenue estimate for 2026 points to a 51% jump over last year. The forecast for 2027 and 2028 is also quite solid, indicating that AMD is on track to become a significantly larger company. The good news for investors is that AMD's revenue growth will filter down to the bottom line as well. AMD EPS Estimates for Current Fiscal Year data by YCharts Finally, when we consider the company's long-term earnings growth potential and valuation, it becomes clear why buying this semiconductor stock amid the recent sell-off could be a smart move. AMD trades at 33 times forward earnings, making it quite attractive given the impressive pace of earnings per share (EPS) growth. It is also worth noting that analysts expect its EPS to grow by nearly 70% annually over the long run. Dallas Area Rapid Transit (DART) is stepping up security and fare enforcement at several light rail stations as part of a new 90-day initiative launching Monday, November 16. Called Operation Access , the program will bring a more visible uniformed presence to key stations across the network, the agency says. Riders will see DART police officers, fare enforcement officers, and transit security officers at designated locations, according to a press release. As part of the initiative, all riders boarding at Pearl/Arts District Station and West End Station will pass through barriers and undergo mandatory fare validation before boarding. Those stations may experience brief delays during peak travel periods, although DART expects any additional wait times to be minimal, they say. In addition to the two downtown stations, uniformed enforcement teams will be stationed at Bachman, Forest Lane, LBJ/Skillman, MLK Jr., and 8th & Corinth stations. Placing officers and security personnel at those locations will create a more consistent presence along key rail corridors while supporting fare compliance and the agency's code of conduct. "At its core, Operation Access is about creating the transit experience our riders deserve," says DART Chief of Police Charles Cato in the release. "When customers see a consistent security presence, know that fares are being checked, and feel confident that everyone is following the same rules, it creates a safer and more comfortable environment for everyone." "When customers see a consistent security presence, know that fares are being checked, and feel confident that everyone is following the same rules, it creates a safer and more comfortable environment for everyone. This first phase allows us to deliver those benefits immediately while gathering the information we need to plan for the future." Gilberto Garza, the assistant chief of DART PD, told CBS News Texas the idea came from changes it put in place for the FIFA World Cup. Dallas Area Rapid Transit (DART) is stepping up security and fare enforcement at several light rail stations as part of a new 90-day initiative launching Monday, November 16. Called Operation Access , the program will bring a more visible uniformed presence to key stations across the network, the agency says. Riders will see DART police officers, fare enforcement officers, and transit security officers at designated locations, according to a press release. As part of the initiative, all riders boarding at Pearl/Arts District Station and West End Station will pass through barriers and undergo mandatory fare validation before boarding. Those stations may experience brief delays during peak travel periods, although DART expects any additional wait times to be minimal, they say. In addition to the two downtown stations, uniformed enforcement teams will be stationed at Bachman, Forest Lane, LBJ/Skillman, MLK Jr., and 8th & Corinth stations. According to DART, the seven stations serve as important entry and exit points for passengers traveling to and from downtown. Placing officers and security personnel at those locations will create a more consistent presence along key rail corridors while supporting fare compliance and the agency's code of conduct. The initiative is intended to improve safety and fare compliance while helping DART better understand how passengers move through the system as it evaluates the possibility of expanding fare-gated access across the light rail network. "At its core, Operation Access is about creating the transit experience our riders deserve," says DART Chief of Police Charles Cato in the release. "When customers see a consistent security presence, know that fares are being checked, and feel confident that everyone is following the same rules, it creates a safer and more comfortable environment for everyone." Cato says the first phase will allow DART to provide those benefits immediately while gathering information to help plan for the future. DART President and CEO Nathaniel P. Ford Sr. also describes Operation Access as an important step in modernizing fare enforcement. "Operation Access allows us to take meaningful action today while planning responsibly for tomorrow," Ford says. "We're making the system safer and improving fare compliance right now, and at the same time we're collecting critical data that will help shape the next generation of rail security and customer experience at DART." Experts at personal finance website WalletHub examined the 100 largest U.S. cities using 18 relevant metrics to determine the best places to "gobble up Thanksgiving festivities at a reasonable price." Cities were also ranked across five main categories: celebrations and traditions; affordability; safety and accessibility; weather forecast; and a "giving thanks" rank. This is the first time Dallas has landed in the top spot; the city previously ranked as the No. 4 best place to go for Thanksgiving in 2025. Dallas ranked No. 2 nationally for its "celebrations and traditions" rank, largely due to its numerous holiday happenings that take over the metroplex in November and December. Additionally, the report said the city is a very attractive locale for those who like to dine out at restaurants. Dallas boasts "an extremely high number of restaurants rated at least 4.5 stars," and it ranks 11th nationally for its dining affordability. Dozens of Dallas-area restaurants are hosting their own Turkey Day feasts this year, and several local hotels are going all out for their festive holiday tea events. extraction.body: Dallas Area Rapid Transit plans to launch a new initiative on Monday aiming to increase security and ensure riders are paying their fares.The initiative, dubbed Operation Access, will see extra uniformed security personnel on duty at seven light rail stations for 90 days. Those will include DART police officers, fare enforcement officers and transit security officers.DART said the effort will also help the agency "better understand how customers move through the system" as it considers adding fare gates to light rail stations in the future."At its core, Operation Access is about creating the transit experience our riders deserve," DART Police Chief Charles Cato said in a statement. "When customers see a consistent security presence, know that fares are being checked, and feel confident that everyone is following the same rules, it creates a safer and more comfortable environment for everyone. This first phase allows us to deliver those benefits immediately while gathering the information we need to plan for the future." Gilberto Garza, the assistant chief of DART PD, told CBS News Texas the idea came from changes it put in place for the FIFA World Cup. "Operation Access was born from our experience with FIFA where we are looking at controlling access at the point of entry to our trains," Garza said.What DART riders can expectRiders boarding at the Pearl/Arts District Station and the West End Station in Downtown Dallas will pass through barriers and will be required to show they paid their fare before getting on the train. DART said those stations may see brief delays during peak travel periods."We're enclosing those platforms, creating a basically a fare zone. extraction.body: Israel's security cabinet convened on Sunday for the first time since early October, holding a three-hour meeting amid concerns over a possible security escalation in the West Bank and preparations for a scenario in which Palestinian Authority security personnel turn their weapons against IDF soldiers and Israeli communities. The IDF's preparations focus on a scenario known as "turning the barrels," in which members of the Palestinian Authority's security services direct their weapons against IDF troops and Israeli communities. The discussion took place after plans developed by the IDF Central Command to address the scenario, which were originally scheduled to be presented to the cabinet in early October, were postponed following a change in the agenda. The IDF has formulated plans to respond to a possible attack by Palestinian security personnel, and the scenario has been rehearsed by the Judea and Samaria Division. IDF Chief of Staff Lt.-Gen. Eyal Zamir previously ordered additional troops to be deployed in the area and preparations to be made for the rapid mobilization of further units if necessary. Defense Minister Israel Katz raised the possibility in October of a large-scale confrontation with the Palestinian Authority, in which members of its security services and the Tanzim organization would act against IDF soldiers and Israeli settlers. According to Katz, Israel could declare war on the Palestinian Authority in such a scenario and launch an offensive in accordance with a plan prepared in advance. Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu also warned of the possibility during a tour of the security barrier along the seam line in Samaria. However, senior IDF officials emphasized in previous discussions that they had no intelligence indicating that Palestinian Authority security personnel intended to carry out such an attack. Central Command chief Maj.-Gen. Avi Bluth also warned that public discussion of the scenario could heighten tensions on the ground. In mid-October, Zamir announced that the IDF would reinforce its deployment in the West Bank , including the deployment of the 98th Division, and stressed the need to be prepared for a transition from defensive operations to offensive action. The IDF also warned of the possibility of an escalation following incidents of violence by Israeli extremists against Palestinians . The cabinet meeting comes during a period of caretaker government, with Netanyahu and Gadi Eisenkot divided over whether significant security decisions should be made during this period. sources.title: Security cabinet meets after six-week hiatus amid fears of West Bank escalation
passages: Israel's security cabinet convened on Sunday for the first time since early October, holding a three-hour meeting amid concerns over a possible security escalation in the West Bank and preparations for a scenario in which Palestinian Authority security personnel turn their weapons against IDF soldiers and Israeli communities.
The cabinet meeting comes during a period of caretaker government, with Netanyahu and Gadi Eisenkot divided over whether significant security decisions should be made during this period.
