extraction.body: Outsiders had little reason to notice when Nvidia’s longtime chief security officer and head of product security stepped down in August. Just two and a half months later, CEO Jensen Huang himself left the company over growing questions about his extramarital relationships — starting with an executive at Megaspeed, a Singapore data center company that U.S. investigators suspect of funneling Nvidia chips to China, then widening to reports about two separate affairs with Nvidia employees. At the time, David Reber, who spent four years as CSO and seven at Nvidia overall, said he was leaving for health reasons. “This wasn’t a pivot I had planned. But I know what needs to come first: family and health,” he wrote on LinkedIn in late August, disclosing that he’d been diagnosed with young-onset Parkinson’s more than two years ago. Reber’s replacement, Saša Zdjelar, previously spent 17 years at ExxonMobil in Houston, leaving as a senior IT manager before spending one year at Salesforce and several years at the cybersecurity company ReversingLabs. Zdjelar didn’t respond to questions Thursday about the transition or what the security team knew. Nothing public connects Reber’s or Zdjelar’s role changes to the Megaspeed matter, but it seems fair to wonder what Nvidia’s security team knew about the government’s scrutiny of Megaspeed and about Huang’s relationships, and whether anyone raised concerns. Reber didn’t respond to questions Thursday. Nvidia also has not answered our related questions. Relationships between a CEO and his employees typically fall to HR, legal and the board, not security. But security specialists say any affair — even one inside the office — can give a foreign intelligence service leverage over an exec who wants it kept quiet. Still, spotting the clues isn’t easy. The way intelligence services collect information, much of it through everyday conversation rather than hacking, makes it especially difficult for security teams to identify risks, according to retired senior intelligence officer Nicholas Eftimiades, who says he has trained more than 1,000 corporate security professionals. Some people inside Nvidia clearly knew parts of the picture. Nvidia’s top lawyer was engaged with the government’s Megaspeed inquiry more than a year ago, The New York Times reported earlier this week . (Nvidia has said it regularly contacts officials.) Reports about Huang’s relationships with employees suggest colleagues also knew of them, even if the behavior is not expressly forbidden by Nvidia’s code of conduct . The Times cited five Nvidia employees who said he was involved with a vice president who reported directly to him; Reuters, citing two people, later reported a second relationship. What’s unclear is whether any of that reached security. Even if it had, Eftimiades, who wrote Chinese Espionage Operations and Tactics in 2020, told TechCrunch that a security team’s resources are often limited. For one thing, they’re often underfunded because, unlike some other cost centers, they don’t drive revenue. It’s astonishingly common for CEOs to answer a security team’s warnings with “not a nickel more than compliance,” he said. Many companies also define security overly narrowly, specialists say. In an opinion piece in The Hill , Don Aviv, CEO of the corporate investigations firm Interfor International, and author Jeremy Hurewitz, wrote, “Too many companies still approach security primarily as a matter of protecting facilities, preventing cyberattacks, and responding to physical threats.” The two argued that “[s]ecurity teams need to pay greater attention to insider threats, including the cultivation of executives and employees by foreign intelligence services, suspicious business relationships, conflicts of interest and attempts to obtain sensitive information through trusted personal contacts.” It would be surprising if Nvidia’s security team didn’t have a more expansive remit than most companies given its scale and business partners, but it’s possible. In fairness, some of it is simply beyond what any team can do. Speaking generally, not about Huang, Eftimiades offered a hypothetical in which a CEO complains that he can’t do something because “I’m fighting a board who doesn’t want to do this.” That tells an intelligence asset who the obstacle is. The service then asks, “Who’s the sticking point here?” and looks for ways into that person’s email and phone. What a rival intelligence service wants is often less technology than policy insight, including who’s pushing to change export rules and who the biggest blocker is. “Intel world tends to be like cancer,” he said. “Once it gets into the body, it looks to spread and looks to reach out.” The playbook isn’t new, Eftimiades added, “particularly for China.” Any executive dealing with the country “will tell you that they’ve been approached.” He said there are also “tons of diplomat stories” of U.S. diplomats walking into a hotel room to find a woman on the bed. He said what’s newer compared with Soviet era spying is the relationships these services cultivate now often last years, not weeks. Technology can augment that human intelligence, Eftimiades said, pointing to IMSI catchers as one example. The devices mimic a cell tower so that nearby phones connect to them. A basic version can cost about $1,000 and fit in a suitcase, he said, though government-grade models cost far more, and there were a couple of cases involving Chinese espionage where these factored in last year. Eftimiades says no one knows yet if the devices were used against Huang, whose phone was presumably hardened such that compromises could be detected, if not stopped altogether. But what Nvidia’s security team knew, and whether it could have acted on it, will only become clearer as the board’s independent investigation and federal inquiries proceed. In the meantime, Eftimiades said he hopes the whole episode is “a wake-up call” for U.S. industry, which he said is mostly “clueless” about China’s tactics. “We have lost trillions [of dollars] in intellectual property,” is his guess. “Whatever we think we’re doing isn’t working.” Get an Early Peek at the Next TechCrunch Disrupt Disrupt, Startup Battlefield, and more will return next year, and you can be at the front of the line. sources.title: ChatGPT’s new Wallet lets AI agents shop and check out for you
passages: On Friday, OpenAI launched a new wallet feature that lets its agents, called dots , help you decide what to buy and then complete the purchase on your behalf.
The option will initially be available to a limited number of U.S.
ChatGPT Pro subscribers, ages 18 and up, with a U.S.-issued Visa, Mastercard, or American Express.

To get started, ChatGPT subscribers add their eligible payment cards to the new ChatGPT Wallet, then ask their dot to help with a purchase. (This setup is a one-time thing; users don’t have to re-enter their payment information every time they buy.) When it’s time to transact, ChatGPT’s Wallet charges the selected card using a payment token, which is a substitute for the user’s actual card details, so that information isn’t shared with either the dot or the merchant.
The addition comes as consumer-facing AI tools are working to find the right product-market fit, in terms of how they can help people be more efficient as they complete various tasks.

While companies like DoorDash and Uber have so far reported low numbers of orders placed by AI agents, Meta’s Muse, which now has over 10 million users, has seen AI-assisted shopping become a top activity on its app.
Other personal AI agents, like Instinct, also support making purchases on users’ behalf.

OpenAI says that users are fully in control of the purchases, as they’re able to review the items, the total, and the payment card that will be used to complete the transaction before the checkout occurs.
In addition, users will approve the purchases directly with a security check like Face ID or a fingerprint, which creates a record of their transaction.
Where was Nvidia’s security team? Connie Loizos

extraction.body: ChatGPT can now shop for you. On Friday, OpenAI launched a new wallet feature that lets its agents, called dots , help you decide what to buy and then complete the purchase on your behalf. The option will initially be available to a limited number of U.S. ChatGPT Pro subscribers, ages 18 and up, with a U.S.-issued Visa, Mastercard, or American Express. OpenAI says that users are fully in control of the purchases, as they’re able to review the items, the total, and the payment card that will be used to complete the transaction before the checkout occurs. In addition, users will approve the purchases directly with a security check like Face ID or a fingerprint, which creates a record of their transaction. The addition comes as consumer-facing AI tools are working to find the right product-market fit, in terms of how they can help people be more efficient as they complete various tasks. While companies like DoorDash and Uber have so far reported low numbers of orders placed by AI agents, Meta’s Muse, which now has over 10 million users, has seen AI-assisted shopping become a top activity on its app. Other personal AI agents, like Instinct, also support making purchases on users’ behalf. It’s no surprise, then, that OpenAI would want to enter this space more with an agentic shopping feature of its own. To get started, ChatGPT subscribers add their eligible payment cards to the new ChatGPT Wallet, then ask their dot to help with a purchase. (This setup is a one-time thing; users don’t have to re-enter their payment information every time they buy.) When it’s time to transact, ChatGPT’s Wallet charges the selected card using a payment token, which is a substitute for the user’s actual card details, so that information isn’t shared with either the dot or the merchant. The merchant will automatically receive what it needs to fulfill the order from the dot, like the shipping address and contact information, OpenAI says. The company notes that customers who shop via their dots will still be able to earn their credit card rewards and be able to take advantage of protections that typically come with cards, like being able to dispute transactions. The limited availability at launch will allow OpenAI to test and improve the feature and its capabilities before rolling it out more broadly. In the future, the company plans to offer users more control over the feature by allowing them to set spending limits or configure other parameters around purchase categories or time periods, so they can pre-approve purchases that their agent can then handle more autonomously. It also aims to make the agentic shopping feature an option at a broader number of supported retailers. This could be a challenge in some areas, where retailers are blocking AI agents from using their site ; on the shopping front, the largest retailer to ban AI agents is Amazon, as it aims to steer users to its own AI agent, Alexa, instead. To help retailers adapt to agentic commerce, OpenAI also published a Commerce Partner Playbook that offers tools and guidance to sites that want to support customers using agents. extraction.body: ChatGPT can now shop for you. On Friday, OpenAI launched a new wallet feature that lets its agents, called dots , help you decide what to buy and then complete the purchase on your behalf. The option will initially be available to a limited number of U.S. ChatGPT Pro subscribers, ages 18 and up, with a U.S.-issued Visa, Mastercard, or American Express. OpenAI says that users are fully in control of the purchases, as they’re able to review the items, the total, and the payment card that will be used to complete the transaction before the checkout occurs. In addition, users will approve the purchases directly with a security check like Face ID or a fingerprint, which creates a record of their transaction. The addition comes as consumer-facing AI tools are working to find the right product-market fit, in terms of how they can help people be more efficient as they complete various tasks. While companies like DoorDash and Uber have so far reported low numbers of orders placed by AI agents, Meta’s Muse, which now has over 10 million users, has seen AI-assisted shopping become a top activity on its app. Other personal AI agents, like Instinct, also support making purchases on users’ behalf. It’s no surprise, then, that OpenAI would want to enter this space more with an agentic shopping feature of its own. To get started, ChatGPT subscribers add their eligible payment cards to the new ChatGPT Wallet, then ask their dot to help with a purchase. (This setup is a one-time thing; users don’t have to re-enter their payment information every time they buy.) When it’s time to transact, ChatGPT’s Wallet charges the selected card using a payment token, which is a substitute for the user’s actual card details, so that information isn’t shared with either the dot or the merchant. The merchant will automatically receive what it needs to fulfill the order from the dot, like the shipping address and contact information, OpenAI says. The company notes that customers who shop via their dots will still be able to earn their credit card rewards and be able to take advantage of protections that typically come with cards, like being able to dispute transactions. The limited availability at launch will allow OpenAI to test and improve the feature and its capabilities before rolling it out more broadly. In the future, the company plans to offer users more control over the feature by allowing them to set spending limits or configure other parameters around purchase categories or time periods, so they can pre-approve purchases that their agent can then handle more autonomously. It also aims to make the agentic shopping feature an option at a broader number of supported retailers. This could be a challenge in some areas, where retailers are blocking AI agents from using their site ; on the shopping front, the largest retailer to ban AI agents is Amazon, as it aims to steer users to its own AI agent, Alexa, instead. To help retailers adapt to agentic commerce, OpenAI also published a Commerce Partner Playbook that offers tools and guidance to sites that want to support customers using agents. sources.title: Why Did Google Pixels Stop Using Snapdragon Chips? - Engadget
passages: It seems like it was just yesterday when Google dropped Qualcomm's Snapdragon chips and launched the Pixel 6 on its proprietary Tensor platform – but it's not.
Qualcomm's flagship phone chips are said to cost manufacturers $240 to $280 per unit in the current Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5 generation.
Alas, while the switch from Snapdragon to Tensor didn't make Pixels cheaper than their rivals, it did give Google what it wanted: its own chip roadmap.

The publication puts this discrepancy down to Google's financial priorities rather than any failures in engineering, but there's no dancing around the fact that a flagship Snapdragon or an Apple A-series chip beats Tensor on things like raw power and sustained gaming loads (and probably battery life under heavy use), and that's been true of every Tensor Pixel since 2021.
The Tensor G6 in the new Google Pixel 11 continues that lineage, while the Pixel Watch 5 that launched beside it still carries a Qualcomm chip.
Google ditched Snapdragon in 2021 to build phones around its own AI silicon.

extraction.body: Google ditched Snapdragon in 2021 to build phones around its own AI silicon. It seems like it was just yesterday when Google dropped Qualcomm's Snapdragon chips and launched the Pixel 6 on its proprietary Tensor platform – but it's not. We've just passed the five(!) year anniversary in October, so what better time than now to look at why Google did it. The decision saw Google swap out the mobile gaming pedigree of Snapdragon in the Pixel 5a for better AI capabilities (like transcribing a rambling voice note) in the Pixel 6 with Tensor silicon shaped around Google's machine learning models. Tensor spent its first four generations as a heavily reworked Samsung Exynos design. Google only recently moved to a chip of its own base design with last year's Tensor G5, fabricated in Taiwan by TSMC. The Tensor G6 in the new Google Pixel 11 continues that lineage, while the Pixel Watch 5 that launched beside it still carries a Qualcomm chip. In August 2021, Google's SVP of Devices and Services, Rick Osterloh, wrote in an announcement that the company had "run into computing limitations that prevented us from fully pursuing our mission" in AI, so it built its own chip. Its centerpiece was the tensor processing unit (TPU), a custom application-specific integrated circuit dedicated to running Google's speech recognition, translation and computational photography models on the phone instead of in the cloud. Five generations on, the workload has changed but the overarching design hasn't; Google says the Tensor G6 packs 50 percent more TPU compute than the G5. Paired with the latest Gemini Nano model, it also claims up to 3.5 times faster on-device AI tasks that use up to 3.5 times less energy. Testing by Android Authority measured Qualcomm's Snapdragon 8 Elite at more than twice the Tensor G5's multi-core CPU performance and around 2.5 times its graphics performance. The publication puts this discrepancy down to Google's financial priorities rather than any failures in engineering, but there's no dancing around the fact that a flagship Snapdragon or an Apple A-series chip beats Tensor on things like raw power and sustained gaming loads (and probably battery life under heavy use), and that's been true of every Tensor Pixel since 2021. Google is a services company before it's a silicon specialist after all, and it has accepted deficits in benchmarks as the price of running its Gemini features the way it wants. That's great if you're a Gemini power user, but not so great if you're any other type of power user. The Pixel Watch 5 was announced alongside the Pixel Tag and Pixel 11 series , and runs on Qualcomm's Snapdragon W5 Gen 2. Indeed, the company hasn't yet made any wearable Tensor products and still relies on Qualcomm's silicon wherever it doesn't use its own. Tensor itself began as a Samsung co-development codenamed Whitechapel. A 2021 analysis of the first chip found that it shared clock management, power management architecture and memory controllers with Samsung's Exynos processors. Samsung was responsible for manufacturing every Tensor through the G4 and supplied the modems, and its processes were blamed for the line's thermal issues and its Exynos modems for the connectivity problems. The Tensor G5 in last year's Pixel 10 was the first one built without Samsung, and the G6 is understood to have swapped the Exynos modem for a MediaTek part. That's according to leaked specifications that have since been partly confirmed , thus removing the last major Samsung part from a platform it helped build. Qualcomm's flagship phone chips are said to cost manufacturers $240 to $280 per unit in the current Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5 generation. That's an increase of $40 to $80 compared to the 8 Gen 3. In designing Tensor, Google has managed to dodge that markup and divert more budget to refining the TPU its AI features are built around. Interestingly, Samsung has gone in the other direction: Its Galaxy S26 Ultra uses that Gen 5 chip across all regions. On top of that, all North American S26 models use Snapdragon. Alas, while the switch from Snapdragon to Tensor didn't make Pixels cheaper than their rivals, it did give Google what it wanted: its own chip roadmap.

Alas, while the switch from Snapdragon to Tensor didn't make Pixels cheaper than their rivals, it did give Google what it wanted: its own chip roadmap.

The publication puts this discrepancy down to Google's financial priorities rather than any failures in engineering, but there's no dancing around the fact that a flagship Snapdragon or an Apple A-series chip beats Tensor on things like raw power and sustained gaming loads (and probably battery life under heavy use), and that's been true of every Tensor Pixel since 2021.
The Tensor G6 in the new Google Pixel 11 continues that lineage, while the Pixel Watch 5 that launched beside it still carries a Qualcomm chip.
Google ditched Snapdragon in 2021 to build phones around its own AI silicon.

extraction.body: Google ditched Snapdragon in 2021 to build phones around its own AI silicon. It seems like it was just yesterday when Google dropped Qualcomm's Snapdragon chips and launched the Pixel 6 on its proprietary Tensor platform – but it's not. We've just passed the five(!) year anniversary in October, so what better time than now to look at why Google did it. The decision saw Google swap out the mobile gaming pedigree of Snapdragon in the Pixel 5a for better AI capabilities (like transcribing a rambling voice note) in the Pixel 6 with Tensor silicon shaped around Google's machine learning models. Tensor spent its first four generations as a heavily reworked Samsung Exynos design. Google only recently moved to a chip of its own base design with last year's Tensor G5, fabricated in Taiwan by TSMC. The Tensor G6 in the new Google Pixel 11 continues that lineage, while the Pixel Watch 5 that launched beside it still carries a Qualcomm chip. In August 2021, Google's SVP of Devices and Services, Rick Osterloh, wrote in an announcement that the company had "run into computing limitations that prevented us from fully pursuing our mission" in AI, so it built its own chip. Its centerpiece was the tensor processing unit (TPU), a custom application-specific integrated circuit dedicated to running Google's speech recognition, translation and computational photography models on the phone instead of in the cloud. Five generations on, the workload has changed but the overarching design hasn't; Google says the Tensor G6 packs 50 percent more TPU compute than the G5. Paired with the latest Gemini Nano model, it also claims up to 3.5 times faster on-device AI tasks that use up to 3.5 times less energy. Testing by Android Authority measured Qualcomm's Snapdragon 8 Elite at more than twice the Tensor G5's multi-core CPU performance and around 2.5 times its graphics performance. The publication puts this discrepancy down to Google's financial priorities rather than any failures in engineering, but there's no dancing around the fact that a flagship Snapdragon or an Apple A-series chip beats Tensor on things like raw power and sustained gaming loads (and probably battery life under heavy use), and that's been true of every Tensor Pixel since 2021. Google is a services company before it's a silicon specialist after all, and it has accepted deficits in benchmarks as the price of running its Gemini features the way it wants. That's great if you're a Gemini power user, but not so great if you're any other type of power user. The Pixel Watch 5 was announced alongside the Pixel Tag and Pixel 11 series , and runs on Qualcomm's Snapdragon W5 Gen 2. Indeed, the company hasn't yet made any wearable Tensor products and still relies on Qualcomm's silicon wherever it doesn't use its own. Tensor itself began as a Samsung co-development codenamed Whitechapel. A 2021 analysis of the first chip found that it shared clock management, power management architecture and memory controllers with Samsung's Exynos processors. Samsung was responsible for manufacturing every Tensor through the G4 and supplied the modems, and its processes were blamed for the line's thermal issues and its Exynos modems for the connectivity problems. The Tensor G5 in last year's Pixel 10 was the first one built without Samsung, and the G6 is understood to have swapped the Exynos modem for a MediaTek part. That's according to leaked specifications that have since been partly confirmed , thus removing the last major Samsung part from a platform it helped build. Qualcomm's flagship phone chips are said to cost manufacturers $240 to $280 per unit in the current Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5 generation. That's an increase of $40 to $80 compared to the 8 Gen 3. In designing Tensor, Google has managed to dodge that markup and divert more budget to refining the TPU its AI features are built around. Interestingly, Samsung has gone in the other direction: Its Galaxy S26 Ultra uses that Gen 5 chip across all regions. On top of that, all North American S26 models use Snapdragon. Alas, while the switch from Snapdragon to Tensor didn't make Pixels cheaper than their rivals, it did give Google what it wanted: its own chip roadmap.

extraction.body: Carpet making may be one of the oldest skilled jobs in the world, but even this traditional industry has begun to adopt the most modern of technologies – Artificial Intelligence (AI). Kukoon Rugs is a family-owned firm that sells online and through some of the biggest retail chains in the UK and Ireland. Chief Executive Paul Vallely says AI allows the business to be more competitive, allowing him to scale up parts of the firm that he previously wouldn't have been able to. "I think every department uses it extensively, pretty much daily. That's from finance through to commercial, marketing, supply chain, and product." While acknowledging the history of his family's business in Newry, he believes technology like AI can only enhance it. "Rug making has been around for thousands of years, and has been around in this area for a long, long time. "The product itself maybe doesn't change too much, but every single bit of the process as to how we design and create the product, market it to the customer, and then get it to the customer, that's fundamentally changing. And that's through AI." Artificial Intelligence has often been accused of having a negative impact on creative industries , but Vallely says this isn't the case. "AI is allowing us to do more accurate, more efficient, and far faster and more thoughtful work, and it's releasing the team's time to look at more analysis, more research, and actually produce more creative work." Vallely says the "biggest impact for us to adopting AI has been, first of all, the removal of some of the very worst and most boring tasks across office-based roles, and probably the excitement and engagement of the team". "I think as everyone started to adopt it and really buy into it, everyone can see opportunities to do work that they were never able to do before to a standard they were never able to do it, and they're really getting their time released to do more." Kukoon is not the only business to harness artificial intelligence in a bid to become more competitive. The manufacturing industry also has a long tradition in Northern Ireland, which became world famous for linen and shipbuilding in the wake of the industrial revolution in the 19th century. Their products are exported to healthcare facilities right across the globe including the US and Australia. Their seats have also featured in television dramas including Emmerdale and Coronation Street. For managing director Martin Tierney, AI has its strengths and weaknesses, but it is now an integrated part of his company's daily work. "AI is not going to replace your job, but someone who knows AI could replace your job, so we're very much embracing it, encouraging people to use it, and doing it within guardrails in a sensible way," Tierney says. While Tierney feels the technology is poor at customer service, it has revolutionised many of the back-office functions. "On all the laborious things like accounting and finance and data and pulling together information from 20 different sources, it's a really good tool to help you get there." Tierney says he likens the power of AI to that of a calculator. "Well, that didn't happen. It allowed the accountant to be more productive, and then Excel came along and made them more productive again. "AI is doing that again, but doing it on steroids." He says implementing AI across his business has not only improved productivity it has also led to new jobs being created. "We have more team members now than we did before, and AI is allowing those people to be more productive, to do more intelligent work, and less of the boring work. "No one likes going upstairs and into a filing cabinet to pull out a drawer and flick through your paper. You know that's not a good use of anyone's time." Tierney says one of the great things about AI is that he doesn't need to have an IT degree to make use of the software. "You just chat to it, say: 'Here's what I'm trying to do, could you help me flesh out this idea?'" While staff at Seating Matters are encouraged to use AI to help solve problems and speed up some of the more mundane tasks, they do operate within guardrails. "We're not putting patient information or financial information on here. "Yes, we can use it to sift through data to help us find an email from six years ago that might be relevant today, but we're doing it in a way that there's always a human at the wheel. It's always checked by someone." There's more on this story on the BBC's The View .

"AI is allowing us to do more accurate, more efficient, and far faster and more thoughtful work, and it's releasing the team's time to look at more analysis, more research, and actually produce more creative work."

Vallely says the "biggest impact for us to adopting AI has been, first of all, the removal of some of the very worst and most boring tasks across office-based roles, and probably the excitement and engagement of the team".

"I think as everyone started to adopt it and really buy into it, everyone can see opportunities to do work that they were never able to do before to a standard they were never able to do it, and they're really getting their time released to do more."
Kukoon is not the only business to harness artificial intelligence in a bid to become more competitive.
The manufacturing industry also has a long tradition in Northern Ireland, which became world famous for linen and shipbuilding in the wake of the industrial revolution in the 19th century.

Their products are exported to healthcare facilities right across the globe including the US and Australia. Their seats have also featured in television dramas including Emmerdale and Coronation Street.

"AI is not going to replace your job, but someone who knows AI could replace your job, so we're very much embracing it, encouraging people to use it, and doing it within guardrails in a sensible way," Tierney says.
While Tierney feels the technology is poor at customer service, it has revolutionised many of the back-office functions.
"On all the laborious things like accounting and finance and data and pulling together information from 20 different sources, it's a really good tool to help you get there."

"Well, that didn't happen. It allowed the accountant to be more productive, and then Excel came along and made them more productive again.

Tierney says one of the great things about AI is that he doesn't need to have an IT degree to make use of the software.
"You just chat to it, say: 'Here's what I'm trying to do, could you help me flesh out this idea?'"

"We're not putting patient information or financial information on here.

"Yes, we can use it to sift through data to help us find an email from six years ago that might be relevant today, but we're doing it in a way that there's always a human at the wheel. It's always checked by someone."

extraction.body: Jensen Huang’s affair with a suspected spy is Silicon Valley’s worst nightmare come true Jensen Huang’s affair with a suspected spy is Silicon Valley’s worst nightmare come true T he resignation this week of Nvidia’s founder and CEO Jensen Huang is one of the most astonishing corporate scandals in memory, featuring allegations of international espionage and extramarital affairs involving one of the world’s most powerful men. As investigations mount into what went wrong at the $4tn chip company, the saga may also become a milestone in the decades-long history of spies infiltrating the US tech industry. Huang admitted to being unfaithful to his wife of 41 years in a letter to employees this past weekend, following a report from the New York Times that the tech mogul had a close relationship with a woman US officials suspect of spying for China’s government. Huang resigned on Thursday after 33 years as CEO amid reports of two additional affairs with Nvidia employees, causing the world’s most valuable chip company’s stock to plummet. The scandal has thrown Nvidia into crisis, cast a pall over the AI boom and even threatened the stability of the US economy. Huang’s downfall is a nightmare scenario for a tech industry that has become increasingly fearful of security threats, and a glimpse into what intelligence experts say is a constant theater of corporate espionage secretly playing out every day throughout the US. “The reason that this is making the news is because obviously you have one of the wealthiest men in the world and one of the highest-profile CEOs in the world,” said Don Aviv, the CEO of corporate intelligence firm Interfor International. “But this happens all the time, across industries.” As the AI boom and geopolitical competition with China have ramped up in recent years, the tech industry and security officials have tried to prevent exactly the type of plot that allegedly ensnared Huang. Corporate intelligence firms, AI companies and US officials have been on alert for espionage operations targeting tech executives – with some major tech firms warning employees to be skeptical of their personal relationships and holding investigations into how executives could be compromised. OpenAI has even held training sessions specifically running through “honeypot” scenarios where a corporate spy or foreign intelligence asset pursues a sexual relationship with company staff in return for information or leverage, according to the Wall Street Journal . Aviv meanwhile estimated that his firm alone has conducted around a dozen investigations for significant companies into schemes involving honeypots, personal relationships, coercion or blackmail over the past three years. Beyond a disastrous lapse in judgment from Huang, experts also describe the affair with a suspected spy as a massive failure of corporate oversight and a remarkable triumph for an alleged foreign influence operation. For all the concerns about digital infrastructure and the growth of cyber-attacks, intelligence analysts say that human error remains the most vulnerable part of most companies. “The honeypot style trap is as old as the earth itself,” said Randy Watt, head of the corporate threat assessment and consulting firm SRW. “It speaks to a consistent weakness in humans that is exploitable. “I guarantee you there are a whole number of executives in powerful corporations that are reviewing their relationships with girlfriends,” Watt added. OpenAI, Meta and Google did not return requests for comment on their security practices. Nvidia did not comment on questions about Huang’s affairs or when the company learned about his involvement with the alleged spy. The Chinese government has denied any involvement in the affair or efforts at corporate espionage, with a Ministry of Foreign Affairs spokesperson earlier this week calling the reports “nothing but a smear against China”. The fallout from allegations that China conducted a high-profile foreign intelligence operation against Huang has had global implications on the market and tech industry, with the Nasdaq falling 4% immediately after Huang’s resignation and Nvidia losing hundreds of billions in market value this week. Yet security experts say that while the impact of the operation is unique, the tactics and goals are not. Silicon Valley, flush with incredibly valuable intellectual property and trade secrets, has long been a prized target for foreign spying operations. Throughout the cold war, Soviet agents conducted a decades-long effort to steal technological secrets from US tech firms, including major chip companies, that involved a complex web of international espionage. “Gaining access to our advanced technology continues to be their top priority,” William Casey, director of the CIA, warned in 1985. Other countries and foreign nationals have also launched their own corporate espionage operations. North Korean spies created two businesses in the US with the intent of spreading malicious software to infect cryptocurrency developers, Reuters and cybersecurity firms reported last year. In October, US authorities arrested a Saudi national accused of planting a sophisticated listening device within the headquarters of OpenAI. In recent years, however, it’s China’s government that has been most prominently accused of a multilayered effort to steal technological capabilities and IP from US tech firms. The alleged Chinese operation involving Huang stood out to security experts, however, for both the extremely high-profile target and its apparent success. Huang was first seen with Alice Huang, a Chinese executive who ran the Singapore-based Megaspeed datacenter firm, in late 2023. The two were together at a bar in Taiwan in 2024 and again at a conference in 2025, by which time the US commerce department was investigating whether Megaspeed was diverting AI chips to China in violation of export controls. In spring of this year, state secretary Marco Rubio oversaw a classified memo reporting that the Nvidia CEO was in a relationship with a suspected Chinese spy based on electronic surveillance of Alice Huang, according to the New York Times . Huang’s relationship with Alice Huang ultimately appears to have helped facilitate the transfer of billions of dollars in advanced Nvidia chips to China. “As an American, it’s not good, but I’m impressed with their skills,” Smith, the former FBI counterintelligence official, said. “What a target and a tremendous job by the Chinese.” Huang was not only the head of what was once the world’s most valuable company, but he is also a close ally of Donald Trump who accompanied the president at White House dinners and on Trump’s official state visit to China. Huang has been an influential voice on tech policy, especially on export control and open source AI model issues, although it is unclear whether his extramarital relationship had any bearing on his views. Trump backed Huang after the scandal, calling him an “honorable guy”. The Trump administration is also facing questions over why Alice Huang’s firm Megaspeed was spared from being placed on a list of companies that pose national security concerns, Axios reported , despite intelligence outlining issues with the company. US commerce secretary Howard Lutnick is under pressure to resign over perceived inaction in response to problems with Megaspeed. Nvidia has since announced that it hired a top US law firm to conduct an investigation into Huang’s relationship with the suspected spy, while Trump stated that the FBI would launch its own probe into the affair. Huang has agreed to testify before Congress and he now faces a lawsuit in California accusing him of misleading shareholders. In order to combat the wave of corporate espionage and foreign influence campaigns, many companies have turned to intelligence and threat assessment firms to harden their security – several of which say they are expecting more demand for their services after the Nvidia scandal. These firms hold training and conduct investigations into what makes a company vulnerable, often focusing on the human elements of security. “Everybody thinks it’s like what we see in Hollywood – surreptitious entry and listening devices and bugs and tails,” said Eduardo Jany, head of global security for a major US corporation. “It’s really more about social engineering.” Malicious actors will seek out staff at companies that hold positions of influence or valuable information, frequently using what is publicly available through social media and data brokers to learn their personal information and create targeted plans. An employee with a substance abuse or gambling problem provides one avenue of exploitation, experts said, while a staffer who is lonely and seeking out relationships offers another kind of vulnerability. Attempts at corporate espionage can also often come in the guise of business opportunities, as it appears was potentially the case with Nvidia and Huang, with spies posing as fellow tech executives or financiers. “They’re looking at easy access and proximity from conferences and customer relationships,” Jany said. “They sidle up to our executives at any events or trade shows, or even make promises of investments.” Corporations will sometimes hire firms to conduct what’s called penetration testing to check for weak points in their security, which involves using simulated attacks to uncover real vulnerabilities. One security expert described an example of his firm following an employee to the parking lot of a grocery store in order to gain access to their car and take a corporate ID card left hanging from their rearview mirror. Dealing with C-suite executives like Huang tends to pose its own unique challenges for security and threat assessment firms, experts said. Top leadership at companies possesses far more autonomy and authority than the average employee, making it harder for underlings to confront them about misconduct or potential risks. CEOs can also be hostile to seeing themselves as fallible, with consultants having to sensitively approach the idea that their personal relationships may not be what they seem. “These are really smart, accomplished people and you don’t want to come across telling them that they don’t know how to behave themselves or that they’re not sophisticated enough to know that they’re being taken advantage of,” said Brian Stephens, president of security risk advisory at the CEO advisory firm Teneo. “It’s a defense mechanism to being told that the way you live your life is going to have to change,” said Elizabeth Buckley, Teneo’s head of cyber and technical solutions. In addition to educating staff on protecting themselves from being exploited, security and risk experts emphasized that companies need robust mechanisms to flag concerns about misconduct or outside threats. One question facing Nvidia is who within the company knew about Huang’s relationships and whether any concerns were raised internally. Several corporate intelligence and security experts said it is unfathomable that someone at Nvidia would not be tracking the CEO’s whereabouts and who he was meeting with, especially on trips abroad. Yet for all the training, oversight and security protocols companies can put in place, experts said that no amount of safeguards can totally replace personal judgment. While looming investigations will seek to answer what went wrong at Nvidia to lead to the current disaster, Huang’s downfall was of his own making. “Jensen Huang lost his mind here,” Smith, the former counterintelligence agent, said. “But that often happens with romantic relationships.”

extraction.body: Jensen Huang is out at Nvidia. Washington is just getting started with him and the company he co-founded. Huang, the leather-jacket-clad CEO of the world's most important chipmaker, resigned from Nvidia on Thursday after revelations that he had an affair with a suspected Chinese spy . But the spy saga is gripping Washington, and lawmakers are preparing for investigations into how the now-ex-CEO's affair may have damaged U.S. artificial intelligence dominance, the national security implications and the executive's close relationship with President Donald Trump and his Cabinet. Republicans will have their chance first during their last six weeks controlling both chambers of Congress. GOP leaders immediately summoned Huang to Capitol Hill and said they would subpoena him if he doesn't agree to show up. In January, Democrats, who are already eager to make their mark with oversight when they take over the U.S. House and Senate, will be in the driver's seat. "In this environment where there's some really high stakes when it comes to our national security, I would expect there would be some follow-up, yeah," Senate Majority Leader John Thune , R-S.D., told reporters at the Capitol on Thursday. Huang and the woman with whom he reportedly had a relationship, Alice Huang, an executive at the Singaporean technology company Megaspeed and an alleged Chinese spy have drawn congressional attention. And Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick has drawn fire after reports this week that he stalled President Donald Trump' s crackdowns on firms routing Nvidia chips to China . Some Congress members have also called for an investigation into the role of the Bureau of Industry and Security, a subagency of the Commerce Department that manages and enforces export controls, in the Huang scandal. The New York Times reported on Monday that Nvidia's general counsel, Tim Teter, claimed in emails to Commerce investigators probing Alice Huang's company that he'd been in touch with Jeffrey Kessler, who leads BIS. The Commerce investigation into Megaspeed, which allegedly smuggled restricted chips to China, was then transferred to the Justice Department. By Thursday night, Senate banking committee Chair Tim Scott , R-S.C., summoned both Huang and Lutnick t o testify before his committee in December. Later that same night, Lutnick had "proactively agreed to appear voluntarily before the Banking Committee to address their questions," Kristen Eichamer, a Commerce Department spokesperson, said in a statement. Scott threatened to subpoena Huang if he does not appear. A banking panel spokesperson did not immediately respond Friday morning when asked if they'd heard from Huang. "Recent reports raise serious concerns about our national security and the protection of sensitive U.S. technology," Scott wrote to Huang. "The American people deserve answers." And with Democrats poised to take control of both chambers come January, the tech mogul's close ties to the White House will add fuel to an already burning fire as the new majority spools up myriad investigations into the Trump administration. Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer , D-N.Y., in a post to X on Thursday, said "Congress must demand answers from Mr. Huang and others at Nvidia about how they may have put U.S. national security at risk." Schumer is in a contested race to become Senate majority leader in the next Congress. The senators who will lead those investigations, and hold subpoena power in the new Congress, are gearing up for Nvidia to take center stage. Sen. Elizabeth Warren , D-Mass., the likely incoming chair of the Senate banking panel, said in a statement Thursday that "Mr. Huang, NVIDIA executives, and NVIDIA's board of directors still owe Congress answers about the company's compliance with U.S. export controls Warren and Sen. Chris Coons , D-Del., the top Democrat on the Senate Foreign Relations subpanel with jurisdiction over East Asia and the Pacific, sent a letter Wednesday to Lutnick, Secretary of State Marco Rubio and White House Chief of Staff Stephen Miller instructing them to preserve all documents and communications related to Nvidia's exports of "advanced AI chips to China or to entities that may divert such chips to China." Even before Democrats take control in January, Huang is expected to appear before Congress. House Foreign Affairs Committee Chair Brian Mast , R-Fla., is actively negotiating for Huang to testify before House committees and told reporters Thursday the Nvidia CEO has agreed to appear in the coming weeks. Details of that testimony are still being worked out, Mast said. It would likely include his committee, as well as the House intelligence panel and the House Permanent Select Committee on China, and it would be under oath and transcribed. It's not clear at this point whether it would be public. "We want to see him basically in a week … Sooner rather than later," Mast told reporters Thursday, adding that he believed it would happen before Thanksgiving. If Huang doesn't willingly appear, Mast said he will subpoena him. Mast, along with House Select China Committee Chair Rep. John Moolenaar, R-Mich., and House Intelligence Committee Chair Rep. Rick Crawford, R-Ark., sent a second request Thursday to Huang and Teter requesting they appear and giving them an 8 p.m. ET Friday deadline to respond. Mast also sent a second request to Kessler. Rep. Josh Gottheimer , D-N.J., a member of the House Intelligence Committee, said Friday during an appearance on CNBC's "The Exchange" that he wants answers from Huang on the national security and export implications of the affair. "From an intelligence committee perspective, you can imagine from an AI perspective, how important this is for our national security, for our critical infrastructure and understand when it comes to chip policy, what exactly got to China and ... did Megaspeed divert chips?" Gottheimer said. The calls for immediate investigation into Huang and Nvidia on the day of his resignation represent a stunning fall from grace in the halls of power for the former CEO. Huang was one of the most effective voices for the AI industry in Washington — able to toggle between leveraging his relationship with Trump and defending his industry from fears about AI's risks to lawmakers. "He is always the TED Talk guy," one senior Democratic staff member who was granted anonymity to describe private meetings they had attended with Huang, told CNBC. "He's really good and articulate, and really good at explaining why AI is important and why it's so important for the United States to be leading here." The staffer said Huang was a "happy warrior" for AI, and stayed longer than scheduled or anticipated for questions from lawmakers. But in the meetings with lawmakers the aide attended, they said Huang did not aggressively push against export controls or get too "deep in the weeds" to really "lobby one way or the other" with the lawmakers. Huang has repeatedly resisted export controls publicly, a move that has rubbed some lawmakers the wrong way. Some lawmakers even lamented the loss of Huang, despite the inevitable buzzsaw he now faces on Capitol Hill. "It's just sad all around," Sen. John Fetterman, D-Pa., said of Huang's resignation. The firm's CEO could be removed with or without cause by a majority vote of directors. But that wasn't in the end needed - the board instead announced Huang had resigned as president, CEO and board member. It thanked him for his "immeasurable contributions" to Nvidia, which it said were "profound". There was no mention of the accusations of adultery. Nvidia Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress will serve as interim CEO . It is less clear is who will replace Huang on a permanent basis. One possibility is Nvidia co-founder Chris Malachowsky. He has been at the company as long as Huang, and for years led its product engineering work. Huang's children, Spencer and Madison, and son-in-law Nico Caprez also work at Nvidia in senior roles, but they are relatively young and inexperienced. And there is also the option of Ian Buck, who runs high-performance computing at the firm. He developed the technology which allowed graphics cards to be used for other computing tasks, which enabled Nvidia to capitalise on the growth of AI. She did not respond to the BBC's request for comment. He has an estimated fortune of $155bn (£115bn), according to the Bloomberg Billionaires Index. Since 2022, the US has used various export controls to keep the top tech out of China, which it says helps retain America's competitive edge and protects its national security. extraction.body: Jensen Huang’s affair with a suspected spy is Silicon Valley’s worst nightmare come true Jensen Huang’s affair with a suspected spy is Silicon Valley’s worst nightmare come true T he resignation this week of Nvidia’s founder and CEO Jensen Huang is one of the most astonishing corporate scandals in memory, featuring allegations of international espionage and extramarital affairs involving one of the world’s most powerful men. As investigations mount into what went wrong at the $4tn chip company, the saga may also become a milestone in the decades-long history of spies infiltrating the US tech industry. Huang admitted to being unfaithful to his wife of 41 years in a letter to employees this past weekend, following a report from the New York Times that the tech mogul had a close relationship with a woman US officials suspect of spying for China’s government. Huang resigned on Thursday after 33 years as CEO amid reports of two additional affairs with Nvidia employees, causing the world’s most valuable chip company’s stock to plummet. The scandal has thrown Nvidia into crisis, cast a pall over the AI boom and even threatened the stability of the US economy. Huang’s downfall is a nightmare scenario for a tech industry that has become increasingly fearful of security threats, and a glimpse into what intelligence experts say is a constant theater of corporate espionage secretly playing out every day throughout the US. “The reason that this is making the news is because obviously you have one of the wealthiest men in the world and one of the highest-profile CEOs in the world,” said Don Aviv, the CEO of corporate intelligence firm Interfor International. “But this happens all the time, across industries.” As the AI boom and geopolitical competition with China have ramped up in recent years, the tech industry and security officials have tried to prevent exactly the type of plot that allegedly ensnared Huang. Corporate intelligence firms, AI companies and US officials have been on alert for espionage operations targeting tech executives – with some major tech firms warning employees to be skeptical of their personal relationships and holding investigations into how executives could be compromised. OpenAI has even held training sessions specifically running through “honeypot” scenarios where a corporate spy or foreign intelligence asset pursues a sexual relationship with company staff in return for information or leverage, according to the Wall Street Journal . Aviv meanwhile estimated that his firm alone has conducted around a dozen investigations for significant companies into schemes involving honeypots, personal relationships, coercion or blackmail over the past three years. Beyond a disastrous lapse in judgment from Huang, experts also describe the affair with a suspected spy as a massive failure of corporate oversight and a remarkable triumph for an alleged foreign influence operation. For all the concerns about digital infrastructure and the growth of cyber-attacks, intelligence analysts say that human error remains the most vulnerable part of most companies. “The honeypot style trap is as old as the earth itself,” said Randy Watt, head of the corporate threat assessment and consulting firm SRW. “It speaks to a consistent weakness in humans that is exploitable. “I guarantee you there are a whole number of executives in powerful corporations that are reviewing their relationships with girlfriends,” Watt added. OpenAI, Meta and Google did not return requests for comment on their security practices. Nvidia did not comment on questions about Huang’s affairs or when the company learned about his involvement with the alleged spy. The Chinese government has denied any involvement in the affair or efforts at corporate espionage, with a Ministry of Foreign Affairs spokesperson earlier this week calling the reports “nothing but a smear against China”. The fallout from allegations that China conducted a high-profile foreign intelligence operation against Huang has had global implications on the market and tech industry, with the Nasdaq falling 4% immediately after Huang’s resignation and Nvidia losing hundreds of billions in market value this week. Yet security experts say that while the impact of the operation is unique, the tactics and goals are not. Silicon Valley, flush with incredibly valuable intellectual property and trade secrets, has long been a prized target for foreign spying operations. Throughout the cold war, Soviet agents conducted a decades-long effort to steal technological secrets from US tech firms, including major chip companies, that involved a complex web of international espionage. “Gaining access to our advanced technology continues to be their top priority,” William Casey, director of the CIA, warned in 1985. Other countries and foreign nationals have also launched their own corporate espionage operations. North Korean spies created two businesses in the US with the intent of spreading malicious software to infect cryptocurrency developers, Reuters and cybersecurity firms reported last year. In October, US authorities arrested a Saudi national accused of planting a sophisticated listening device within the headquarters of OpenAI. In recent years, however, it’s China’s government that has been most prominently accused of a multilayered effort to steal technological capabilities and IP from US tech firms. The alleged Chinese operation involving Huang stood out to security experts, however, for both the extremely high-profile target and its apparent success. extraction.body: Jensen Huang is out at Nvidia. Washington is just getting started with him and the company he co-founded. Huang, the leather-jacket-clad CEO of the world's most important chipmaker, resigned from Nvidia on Thursday after revelations that he had an affair with a suspected Chinese spy . But the spy saga is gripping Washington, and lawmakers are preparing for investigations into how the now-ex-CEO's affair may have damaged U.S. artificial intelligence dominance, the national security implications and the executive's close relationship with President Donald Trump and his Cabinet. Republicans will have their chance first during their last six weeks controlling both chambers of Congress. GOP leaders immediately summoned Huang to Capitol Hill and said they would subpoena him if he doesn't agree to show up. In January, Democrats, who are already eager to make their mark with oversight when they take over the U.S. House and Senate, will be in the driver's seat. "In this environment where there's some really high stakes when it comes to our national security, I would expect there would be some follow-up, yeah," Senate Majority Leader John Thune , R-S.D., told reporters at the Capitol on Thursday. Huang and the woman with whom he reportedly had a relationship, Alice Huang, an executive at the Singaporean technology company Megaspeed and an alleged Chinese spy have drawn congressional attention. And Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick has drawn fire after reports this week that he stalled President Donald Trump' s crackdowns on firms routing Nvidia chips to China . Some Congress members have also called for an investigation into the role of the Bureau of Industry and Security, a subagency of the Commerce Department that manages and enforces export controls, in the Huang scandal. The New York Times reported on Monday that Nvidia's general counsel, Tim Teter, claimed in emails to Commerce investigators probing Alice Huang's company that he'd been in touch with Jeffrey Kessler, who leads BIS. The Commerce investigation into Megaspeed, which allegedly smuggled restricted chips to China, was then transferred to the Justice Department. By Thursday night, Senate banking committee Chair Tim Scott , R-S.C., summoned both Huang and Lutnick t o testify before his committee in December. Later that same night, Lutnick had "proactively agreed to appear voluntarily before the Banking Committee to address their questions," Kristen Eichamer, a Commerce Department spokesperson, said in a statement. Scott threatened to subpoena Huang if he does not appear. A banking panel spokesperson did not immediately respond Friday morning when asked if they'd heard from Huang. Huang's children, Spencer and Madison, and son-in-law Nico Caprez also work at Nvidia in senior roles, but they are relatively young and inexperienced. Senate banking committee member Kevin Cramer , R-N.D., doubled down Wednesday on his call for Huang to resign, and a key Democratic House oversight panel member and House Republican piled on. "As a matter of his own conscience, he should resign," Cramer told CNBC, in response to revelations that Huang had an affair with an alleged Chinese spy as the chipmaker he co-founded was given permission from the U.S. government to sell its technology to China. Huang, who leads a company that's been a chief beneficiary of the artificial intelligence boom, on Sunday admitted to having an affair with a woman whom news outlets have reported U.S. intelligence concluded was a Chinese spy . The revelation is sending shockwaves through Washington, with lawmakers now fearing that U.S. AI dominance could be at risk. "What bothers me at the end of it is what we don't know is what she knows about him that can be utilized," Cramer said, referring to Alice Huang and Jensen Huang, who are not related. "This is a guy that's right now so vulnerable to extortion, blackmail. I just don't think, as a national security matter, we can run the risk." Cramer's comments come on the deadline set by a trio of House lawmakers who requested Huang to testify before their committees on Nov. 18. GOP Reps. Brian Mast, chair of the House Foreign Affairs Committee; John Moolenaar, chair of the Permanent Select Committee on China; and Rick Crawford, who leads the House intelligence panel, called for Huang to appear in a Nov. 4 letter . Congress members in the majority party also have subpoena power, should they choose to use it. Mast and Moolenaar told reporters on Wednesday afternoon that they had not yet heard from Huang and that they were giving him until the end of the day to respond. Asked whether the committees were considering subpoenaing Huang if he doesn't agree to appear, Mast said "yes." Moolenaar, when asked the same question, said "all three committees have subpoena power, and I know all three committees have a very serious interest in getting to the bottom of this and having transparency around this." "We are going to continue to pursue this," Moolenaar said. The lawmakers are far from alone in their criticism, concern and outright shock over the affair. And the scrutiny is only expected to intensify with Democrats poised to take over both chambers of Congress in January. Huang has been close with President Donald Trump during the president's second term, traveling on Air Force One to China in May. "Jensen Huang should resign from Nvidia," Rep. Suhas Subramanyam, D-Va., a member of the House Oversight Committee, told CNBC. Subramanyam is the top Democrat on the panel's Subcommittee on Military and Foreign Affairs. "I didn't agree with his sentiment that there's no downside to exporting chips to China," he said. "But I never thought that he might be having an affair with a Chinese spy who was helping smuggle chips into China at an alarming rate." Rep. Don Bacon , R-Neb., who is retiring from Congress after sometimes bucking Trump, also said the CEO should step down. "From the little I know, yes." Bacon told CNBC in response to whether Huang should resign. "I mean, he allowed himself to get compromised by the Chinese government. Not good." Huang was notably opposed to strict export controls on AI chips to China, which ruffled feathers with China hawks on Capitol Hill. Nvidia is now likely to be at the center of those probes. "There's two parts to this investigation that [need] to happen somewhere immediately," Subramanyam said. Rep. The measures are the AI Overwatch Act, which would give Congress power over advanced chip exports, the Chip Security Act, which would require businesses to track their chips to combat smuggling, and the Match Act, which would push US allies to restrict more chipmaking equipment to China. NEW YORK, Nov 9 (Reuters) - Congress is more likely to pass legislation aimed at tightening China's access to AI chips in light of news that Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang had a relationship with a suspected ‌Chinese intelligence agent, lawmakers and advocates said.

Three chip-related measures are slated for possible inclusion in the annual defense authorization ‌bill for fiscal year 2027, which began in October. Huang's affair, and his close relationship with President Donald Trump, has added new urgency to concerns about China's ​access to advanced chips that could undermine US national security.

The measures are the AI Overwatch Act, which would give Congress power over advanced chip exports, the Chip Security Act, which would require businesses to track their chips to combat smuggling, and the Match Act, which would push US allies to restrict more chipmaking equipment to China.
Nvidia is considered the biggest opponent of both the Chip Security and AI Overwatch ‌acts, according to one former congressional staffer ⁠who had direct contact with the company over several months.
Until the US Department of Justice brought indictments tied to chip smuggling last year, Huang and Nvidia had argued there was no such smuggling. The ⁠company said it complied with export laws.
The House Foreign Affairs Committee advanced all three bills earlier this year. They are now in the Senate National Defense Authorization Act management package.

In a joint statement on Monday, Democratic Senator Elizabeth Warren of Massachusetts and her Republican colleague ​Jim ​Banks of Indiana said that "Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's confirmation of a relationship ​with a suspected spy for China's intelligence service makes ‌these national security concerns even more urgent."
They added: "It is time for Congress to take decisive action to pass key bills like the AI Overwatch Act in the NDAA that will cut off pathways through which China accesses advanced chips."
In March, the senators had urged the Department of Commerce to suspend or reconsider Nvidia's export licenses to China and conduct a full security review.

Democratic Representative Bill Foster of Illinois echoed the senators' sentiments. "Congress has the tools to prevent powerful AI chips from getting in the wrong hands and posing a ‌national security risk," Foster posted on X on Monday, in response to ​news of Huang's affair.

He said the Chip Security Act he introduced with Republican ​Representative Bill Huizenga of Michigan had passed unanimously out of ​committee in the House. "It's time to get it across the finish line," he said.

"The hurdle these bills ‌need to clear is getting the White House onboard," said ​Chris MacKenzie, a spokesman for Americans ​for Responsible Innovation, a Washington nonprofit organization that favors the measures. "With everything that's surfaced, it would be costly for the White House to back Nvidia in a fight with Congress over restricting Chinese access to chips."
The White House did not ​comment on the measures.

The Information Technology Industry ‌Council, whose members include Nvidia, among other groups, has opposed the measures, arguing they could undermine US competitiveness and ​complicate export control policy. A spokeswoman for the council declined comment on the current Nvidia situation.
(Reporting by Karen ​Freifeld in New York; editing by Chris Sanders and David Gaffen)

passages: US lawmakers are pressing their colleagues to pass at least four Bills on chip export
US HOUSE Speaker Mike Johnson said on Thursday (Nov 12) there was growing consensus in Congress on limiting chip exports to China after a spy scandal forced out Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang.
Huang stepped down after reports of a romantic relationship with a businesswoman whom US authorities suspect of spying for the Chinese government.

Lawmakers from both parties have since called for tougher restrictions on China’s access to advanced AI chips, threatening access to chips that underpin China’s surging AI development. And senior White House officials were discussing whether Commerce ​Secretary Howard Lutnick should be pushed out, two people familiar with the situation said, as the desire to take action rose across Washington.

A growing number of lawmakers have criticised Lutnick for the administration’s refusal to add dozens of Chinese companies to a key US trade blacklist, and over whether the government was properly overseeing Nvidia’s exports to China.

Nvidia’s advanced AI chips are widely used to develop cutting-edge AI models, making the company key to the US race against China to build superior AI systems. The US has sought for years to limit China’s access to Nvidia’s chips because it does not want the Chinese military to benefit from them.

“The export controls on chips to China has been a big issue around here,” Johnson, a Louisiana Republican, told reporters at the US Capitol, adding he favoured limiting China’s access to the advanced technology. “I think there’s a developing consensus in Congress that is an important position to take.”

The Chinese businesswoman, Alice Huang, was an executive at Megaspeed, an Nvidia partner the US government suspects of helping China obtain advanced AI chips restricted under US export controls. Beijing has denied Alice Huang is a spy.
The case has revived claims among China critics in Washington that US export policies are too weak, boosting calls for more restrictions.

Reuters reported that Chinese AI companies are trying to rent ​Nvidia-powered computing capacity outside China because they are worried the Jensen Huang allegations could spur Washington to tighten restrictions on their ability to access the company’s chips remotely.

Congressional Republicans are keen to attach new restrictions on exporting advanced AI chips to China in the annual defence authorisation Bill, a must-pass measure that funds the military and typically ​attracts bipartisan support, according to a Senate aide, who spoke on the condition of anonymity.

Lawmakers are pressing their colleagues to pass at least four Bills on chip exports, according to statements since Monday. The AI Overwatch Act would give Congress more power over advanced AI chip exports. The Chip Security Act would require ​companies to track the location of advanced AI processors to prevent smuggling.

The Match Act would pressure US allies to restrict sales and maintenance of advanced chipmaking equipment destined for China. The Remote Access Security Act would give the Commerce Department the tools to stop Chinese firms from renting overseas data centres to access Nvidia chips.

Huang’s resignation is unlikely to end congressional scrutiny of Nvidia and could leave the former chief executive more exposed to investigation, said Sunny Cheung, an analyst at the Washington-based Jamestown Foundation.
“Congress can still subpoena him and Nvidia should conduct an independent investigation to determine whether the problems extend beyond Huang,” Cheung said.

Cheung said Huang’s departure could weaken Nvidia’s influence in Washington and create additional momentum for legislation that tightens restrictions on advanced chip exports. He said Nvidia’s new leadership could also reconsider the company’s China strategy as it seeks to rebuild trust with US policymakers.

Jensen Huang is separately expected to testify before Congress before Thanksgiving, which falls on Nov 26. House Foreign Affairs chairman Brian Mast, a Florida Republican, told reporters on Thursday that congressional staff spoke with Nvidia on Wednesday night about a date and location for his testimony.
Mast and two other leading House Republicans asked Huang last week to brief them behind closed doors about his relationship with Alice Huang. REUTERS

Suhas Subramanyam, D-Va., a member of the House Oversight Committee, told CNBC.
Subramanyam is the top Democrat on the panel's Subcommittee on Military and Foreign Affairs.
"There's two parts to this investigation that [need] to happen somewhere immediately," Subramanyam said.

"As a matter of his own conscience, he should resign," Cramer told CNBC, in response to revelations that Huang had an affair with an alleged Chinese spy as the chipmaker he co-founded was given permission from the U.S. government to sell its technology to China.
"What bothers me at the end of it is what we don't know is what she knows about him that can be utilized," Cramer said, referring to Alice Huang and Jensen Huang, who are not related.
"This is a guy that's right now so vulnerable to extortion, blackmail.
I just don't think, as a national security matter, we can run the risk."
Members of Congress are calling on Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang to resign, and momentum is building to subpoena the executive, whose company is a leader in advanced artificial intelligence chips.
"I mean, he allowed himself to get compromised by the Chinese government.

Huang has been close with President Donald Trump during the president's second term, traveling on Air Force One to China in May.

NEW YORK, Nov 9 (Reuters) - Congress is more likely to pass legislation aimed at tightening China's access to AI chips in light of news that Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang had a relationship with a suspected ‌Chinese intelligence agent, lawmakers and advocates said.
Three chip-related measures are slated for possible inclusion in the annual defense authorization ‌bill for fiscal year 2027, which began in October.

"The hurdle these bills ‌need to clear is getting the White House onboard," said ​Chris MacKenzie, a spokesman for Americans ​for Responsible Innovation, a Washington nonprofit organization that favors the measures.
In March, the senators had urged the Department of Commerce to suspend or reconsider Nvidia's export licenses to China and conduct a full security review.
They added: "It is time for Congress to take decisive action to pass key bills like the AI Overwatch Act in the NDAA that will cut off pathways through which China accesses advanced chips."
Until the US Department of Justice brought indictments tied to chip smuggling last year, Huang and Nvidia had argued there was no such smuggling.
The ⁠company said it complied with export laws.
Nvidia is considered the biggest opponent of both the Chip Security and AI Overwatch ‌acts, according to one former congressional staffer ⁠who had direct contact with the company over several months.
"Congress has the tools to prevent powerful AI chips from getting in the wrong hands and posing a ‌national security risk," Foster posted on X on Monday, in response to ​news of Huang's affair.

Johnson has also said that he personally supports efforts to restrict China’s access to powerful AI chips from companies like Nvidia.

The Match Act would pressure US allies to restrict sales and maintenance of advanced chipmaking equipment destined for China.
The Remote Access Security Act would give the Commerce Department the tools to stop Chinese firms from renting overseas data centres to access Nvidia chips.

Reuters reported that Chinese AI companies are trying to rent ​Nvidia-powered computing capacity outside China because they are worried the Jensen Huang allegations could spur Washington to tighten restrictions on their ability to access the company’s chips remotely.

A growing number of lawmakers have criticised Lutnick for the administration’s refusal to add dozens of Chinese companies to a key US trade blacklist, and over whether the government was properly overseeing Nvidia’s exports to China.
Cheung said Huang’s departure could weaken Nvidia’s influence in Washington and create additional momentum for legislation that tightens restrictions on advanced chip exports.
“Congress can still subpoena him and Nvidia should conduct an independent investigation to determine whether the problems extend beyond Huang,” Cheung said.
Jensen Huang is separately expected to testify before Congress before Thanksgiving, which falls on Nov 26.
House Foreign Affairs chairman Brian Mast, a Florida Republican, told reporters on Thursday that congressional staff spoke with Nvidia on Wednesday night about a date and location for his testimony.

Huang’s resignation is unlikely to end congressional scrutiny of Nvidia and could leave the former chief executive more exposed to investigation, said Sunny Cheung, an analyst at the Washington-based Jamestown Foundation.
The case has revived claims among China critics in Washington that US export policies are too weak, boosting calls for more restrictions.
