AMD's earnings growth potential and valuation point to a nice surge in its stock price through the end of the decade.

The past few months haven't been pretty for semiconductor stocks, as evidenced by the 12% decline in the PHLX Semiconductor Sector index over the past three months. Even Advanced Micro Devices (NASDAQ:AMD) has been caught up in this vortex, experiencing significant volatility amid concerns about the sustainability of artificial intelligence (AI) infrastructure spending, which has been key to the growth of the semiconductor sector.

However, the recent weakness in the semiconductor sector has opened up a great opportunity for investors to buy a top stock at an attractive valuation. AMD is emerging as one of the most important players in the AI chip ecosystem, and I won't be surprised to see it embark on a stunning long-term rally.

Missed AI’s "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 15x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we’re only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »
Let's see why I think that AMD could be one of the best AI stocks you can buy right now.

AMD's Epyc server central processing units (CPUs) are in tremendous demand from hyperscalers and AI companies. As a result, the company's data center revenue jumped by 97% year over year in Q3 to $8.5 billion. The good news for AMD investors is that its data center segment has incredible room for growth.

Alphabet 's (NASDAQ:GOOG) (NASDAQ:GOOGL) Google Cloud division has expanded its partnership with AMD to deploy the latter's 5th-generation Epyc server CPUs, security fabric, and x86 software to power its cloud Tensor Processing Unit (TPU) systems. AMD Epyc will serve as the foundation for Google's TPUs, allowing users to run inference applications.

The good news for AMD investors is that Alphabet is poised to spend aggressively on its cloud computing infrastructure. After all, the Google Cloud business reported a backlog of a whopping $561 billion at the end of the third quarter. The tech giant expects to recognize half of that backlog in the next two years, which explains why its capital expenditure is ballooning .

AMD, therefore, is going to be a direct beneficiary of Alphabet's enormous spending. Not surprisingly, the company expects its growth to accelerate at a solid clip. AMD expects revenue to increase by more than 80% in 2027, fueled by healthy growth in the data center business, where it sees the server CPU total addressable market (TAM) jump to $220 billion by 2030.

Importantly, AMD is well-positioned to capitalize on this massive opportunity. It has partnerships with major hyperscalers and AI companies, including OpenAI, Anthropic , Meta Platforms , Microsoft , and others, in the data center segment. These customers should ensure solid long-term revenue growth for AMD, which is precisely what analysts are expecting.
AMD Revenue Estimates for Current Fiscal Year data by YCharts

The $52.2 billion revenue estimate for 2026 points to a 51% jump over last year. The forecast for 2027 and 2028 is also quite solid, indicating that AMD is on track to become a significantly larger company. The good news for investors is that AMD's revenue growth will filter down to the bottom line as well.
AMD EPS Estimates for Current Fiscal Year data by YCharts
Finally, when we consider the company's long-term earnings growth potential and valuation, it becomes clear why buying this semiconductor stock amid the recent sell-off could be a smart move.

AMD trades at 33 times forward earnings, making it quite attractive given the impressive pace of earnings per share (EPS) growth. It is also worth noting that analysts expect its EPS to grow by nearly 70% annually over the long run.
Before you buy stock in Advanced Micro Devices, consider this:

The Motley Fool Stock Advisor analyst team just identified what they believe are the 10 best stocks for investors to buy now… and Advanced Micro Devices wasn’t one of them. The 10 stocks that made the cut could produce monster returns in the coming years.

Consider when Netflix made this list on December 17, 2004... if you invested $1,000 at the time of our recommendation, you’d have $335,171 !* Or when Nvidia made this list on April 15, 2005... if you invested $1,000 at the time of our recommendation, you’d have $1,000,640 !*
*Stock Advisor returns as of November 15, 2026.

Harsh Chauhan has no position in any of the stocks mentioned. The Motley Fool has positions in and recommends Advanced Micro Devices, Alphabet, Meta Platforms, and Microsoft. The Motley Fool has a disclosure policy .

Dallas Area Rapid Transit (DART) is stepping up security and fare enforcement at several light rail stations as part of a new 90-day initiative launching Monday, November 16. Called Operation Access , the program will bring a more visible uniformed presence to key stations across the network, the agency says. Riders will see DART police officers, fare enforcement officers, and transit security officers at designated locations, according to a press release. As part of the initiative, all riders boarding at Pearl/Arts District Station and West End Station will pass through barriers and undergo mandatory fare validation before boarding. Dallas Area Rapid Transit (DART) is stepping up security and fare enforcement at several light rail stations as part of a new 90-day initiative launching Monday, November 16. Called Operation Access , the program will bring a more visible uniformed presence to key stations across the network, the agency says. Riders will see DART police officers, fare enforcement officers, and transit security officers at designated locations, according to a press release. As part of the initiative, all riders boarding at Pearl/Arts District Station and West End Station will pass through barriers and undergo mandatory fare validation before boarding. Those stations may experience brief delays during peak travel periods, although DART expects any additional wait times to be minimal, they say. In addition to the two downtown stations, uniformed enforcement teams will be stationed at Bachman, Forest Lane, LBJ/Skillman, MLK Jr., and 8th & Corinth stations. According to DART, the seven stations serve as important entry and exit points for passengers traveling to and from downtown. Placing officers and security personnel at those locations will create a more consistent presence along key rail corridors while supporting fare compliance and the agency's code of conduct. The initiative is intended to improve safety and fare compliance while helping DART better understand how passengers move through the system as it evaluates the possibility of expanding fare-gated access across the light rail network. "At its core, Operation Access is about creating the transit experience our riders deserve," says DART Chief of Police Charles Cato in the release. "When customers see a consistent security presence, know that fares are being checked, and feel confident that everyone is following the same rules, it creates a safer and more comfortable environment for everyone." Cato says the first phase will allow DART to provide those benefits immediately while gathering information to help plan for the future. DART President and CEO Nathaniel P. Ford Sr. also describes Operation Access as an important step in modernizing fare enforcement. "Operation Access allows us to take meaningful action today while planning responsibly for tomorrow," Ford says. "We're making the system safer and improving fare compliance right now, and at the same time we're collecting critical data that will help shape the next generation of rail security and customer experience at DART." extraction.body: The report demonstrates that the ethnic cleansing campaign in Area C is state-sanctioned, state-driven and state-implemented; it seeks to accelerate the Israeli government’s annexation agenda and settlement expansion through war crimes and crimes against humanity. As such, the report’s conclusions demand that the international community fully confront and name the Israeli state-driven project, and act decisively to prevent the destruction of Palestinian communities and the annexation of the West Bank. Zanuta is one of 117 predominantly Bedouin and herding Palestinian communities in the occupied West Bank that have faced either full or partial displacement due to settler attacks and related access restrictions between January 2023 and April 2026, according to the United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA). In total, approximately 5,910 people were forced to leave their homes, leaving behind them vast, depopulated areas. Most of the affected communities lie in Area C, which comprises over 60% of the West Bank, and has been central to Israel’s territorial and demographic quest for domination for decades because of its natural resources, vital grazing and agricultural land and small Palestinian population. In late December 2022, Benjamin Netanyahu’s Likud party formed Israel’s 37th government in coalition with two ultra nationalist and religious political parties. While state-supported settler violence has been a growing concern over the past three decades for Palestinian communities in the West Bank, there has been an unprecedented surge in the scale and intensity of attacks since then. Since 1967, Israel has been enforcing its occupation through military orders and regulations. The situation in the OPT, including in Area C of the West Bank, is therefore primarily governed by international humanitarian law (including the rules of the law of occupation); and international human rights law. The same international norms apply to occupied East Jerusalem, illegally annexed by Israel since 1967, despite Israel’s attempts to separate it from the rest of the West Bank through a regime of fragmentation and legal segregation. In this report, Amnesty International presents conclusive evidence that these violations, perpetrated between January 2023 and December 2025, amount to the war crime of unlawful deportation and transfer and the crime against humanity of forcible transfer or deportation , committed as part of a policy to ethnically cleanse Area C of the occupied West Bank by forcibly displacing Palestinian Bedouin and herding communities and expanding illegal settlements at their expense. Amnesty International uses the term ethnic cleansing in this report to describe a deliberate pattern of conduct aimed at permanently removing Palestinian Bedouin and herding communities from specific areas of the occupied West Bank, in particular Area C. While ethnic cleansing is not recognized as an independent crime under international law, Amnesty International uses the term in line with the UN Commission of Experts on Former Yugoslavia’s definition, which describes it as “a purposeful policy designed by one ethnic or religious group to remove by violent and terror-inspiring means the civilian population of another ethnic or religious group from certain geographic areas.” While this report covers the period between December 2022 and December 2025, these egregious crimes are ongoing and are part and parcel of Israel’s system of apartheid, as shown by Amnesty International’s continuous documentation and reporting of the situation on the ground. To reach these conclusions, Amnesty International first established Israel’s intent to formalize the annexation of Area C under Israeli law and change its demographic composition, including through violations of international law, constituting war crimes and crimes against humanity. This involved extensive analysis of Israel’s historical annexation-oriented policies, government agreements, official statements by cabinet ministers, proposed and adopted legislation, and governance changes in the occupied West Bank. The organization then assessed how these policies affected Palestinians from Bedouin and herding communities, focusing on three emblematic areas in Area C that had either faced settler-driven displacement or were at risk of such displacement between 2023 and 2025: The report also draws on field and desk research into events that occurred in 22 other Bedouin and herding communities. February 2026 : Israeli authorities re-established a new land registration mechanism that transferred authority over mapping and land measurement in unregistered areas from the Civil Administration to the Ministry of Justice. By the end of that month, Israeli authorities had seized half of the unregistered land in Area C, which accounts for 58% of the area. The security cabinet approved additional measures to entrench Israeli control over Palestinian land. These included: repealing a Jordanian-era law which had prevented non-Palestinians from purchasing land in the West Bank without permission from Palestinian authorities; and reviving a mechanism – through a body within the Civil Administration – that enables the Israeli state to purchase land directly from Palestinians without seeking additional approval. The government also authorized simplified settlement approval procedures. Since it came to power, the government exponentially increased funding to implement the settler movement’s agenda, using the Hamas-led attacks on 7 October 2023 to significantly escalate aggressive annexation-related measures and practices in the West Bank. Makhoul has faced similar displacement dynamics over a longer period. Once home to dozens of families, the community was reduced to four families following the demolition of all 58 structures in 2013 and further demolitions since. Now surrounded by military bases, settlements and outposts, residents describe constant intimidation. Since late 2023, settler violence has escalated sharply, targeting livestock through assaults on shepherds, arson attacks, animal theft, vehicles driven into herds and threats against children. The community has also faced repeated settler trespass, harassment and construction near homes, alongside systematic nighttime grazing by settlers that destroys crops. Residents say they live in fear that any short absence would lead to permanent land seizure. This policy is implemented through the forcible displacement of Palestinian Bedouin and herding communities, acts that amount to the war crime of unlawful deportation and transfer, and the crime against humanity of forcible transfer or deportation, as well as the creation and expansion of settlements, which amount to the war crime of unlawful transfer. In September 2024, the UN General Assembly passed a resolution demanding that Israel end its unlawful presence in the OPT within 12 months, in compliance with the ICJ’s historic opinion outlining third states’ obligations arising from Israel’s unlawful occupation of Palestinian territory. It urged states not to render aid or assistance to Israel’s unlawful presence in any diplomatic, political, legal, military, economic, commercial and financial dealings with Israel. Among other measures, it called for targeted sanctions against individuals and entities engaged in maintaining the occupation, including in relation to settler violence, an end to imports from Israeli settlements and a halt to arms transfers. “We need to establish sovereignty… We are a right-wing government, we were elected, among other things, for this… We need to establish sovereignty… because this is our home, because this is our land, and because we need to tell the whole world: ‘this is ours forever and ever.’ We have another year for this government and now is the time. Sovereignty, and also encouraging [Palestinian] voluntary emigration, which we should do also in Judea and Samaria… If we change the concept and understand that this is our state and our land, everything will be simpler. We did it in the prisons, in establishing the emergency response teams, in demolishing homes in the Negev, in establishing the National Guard, in the arms reform, and now I want Netanyahu to do it with sovereignty and encouraging emigration.” [90] Also in September 2025, Minister of Finance Bezalel Smotrich revealed plans to annex 82% of the West Bank to prevent the establishment of a Palestinian state and to foster Jewish demographic hegemony. [91] In a video clip posted by a reporter for Israeli Channel 14 who attended the event, Smotrich said he rejects “partial sovereignty” and calls for “applying [Israeli] sovereignty over all the land [of the West Bank on which Israeli settlement blocs are built], except for Arab population concentrations,” in line with Israel’s long-standing policy of achieving and maintaining Jewish demographic hegemony in areas under its control. Media circulated an official map bearing the Settlement Administration’s logo, stating the pledge: “maximum land, minimum Arab population.” [92] A year earlier, he had publicly vowed to “bring a million settlers” to the West Bank in response to the State of Palestine’s efforts to strengthen its international recognition. [93] Some of these statements were made to increase popularity, political votes or to appease the coalition parties’ political base. Others reflect some differences between coalition parties. But what is consistent is the overall annexationist drive, which was largely translated into cabinet decisions and concrete actions on the ground. Ze’ev Hever, head of the settler organization Amana, [274] e xplained their purpose in a 2024 interview, saying that “the protection of open areas [in the West Bank] is Amana’s central mission.” [275] Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich explained in December 2024 the importance of herding outposts in taking over land in the West Bank: “Farms [are] a mega-strategic tool for preserving land… You take a farmer, a thousand cows, a penny and a half of investment, you save 40,000 dunums [4,000 hectares]… I estimate that within a few months there will be a model that will allow the vast majority of farms to be regulated. The system will open the door to investing, to arranging water infrastructure, electricity, participation in grazing grants. [276] In 2022, a report by Kerem Navot, an NGO that monitors and researches Israeli land policy in the West Bank, found that illegal settler outposts across the West Bank controlled an estimated 240,000 dunums, amounting to nearly 7% of Area C (4% of the whole West Bank). [277] By the end of 2024, settler outpost control had grown to approximately 746,000 dunums, representing 22% of Area C (13% of the West Bank), according to a joint report by Peace Now and Kerem Navot. [278] The organizations estimated that within only two-and-a-half years, Israeli settlers seized, through herding outposts, 70% of all the land they had taken since the 1990s. [279] The report revealed that the Israeli state supports herding settlers through “land allocation contracts”, which have facilitated the transfer of control over tens of thousands of dunums of land designated as Israeli military “firing zones”, nature reserves and “state land”, as well as privately owned Palestinian lands, into the hands of settler herding outposts. [280] Israel’s allocations of land to its own population illegally transferred to the occupied territory constitute a blatant violation of international law. Rasheed Khudeiri, a farmer from Bardala in the northern Jordan Valley, who coordinates the Jordan Valley Solidarity Campaign, explained how the takeovers happen: “Herding outposts might occupy… only a few dunums each, but through grazing they take over huge areas… A settler from an outpost near Bardala practically seized 500 dunums between 2024 and 2025 by taking his cows to graze there, while at the same time preventing us from accessing this land which we depend on for our livelihood.” [281] For years, Israeli authorities and forces have failed to prevent, and have condoned, facilitated or directly participated in settler violence against Palestinians. Under the 37th government, this support has reached new levels. In response to Amnesty International’s letter to the Ministry of Defense seeking information on whether the Israeli military takes any measures to protect Palestinian Bedouin and herding communities from acts of violence and harassment by Israeli settlers, the army spokesperson’s unit made it clear that its law enforcement actions were primarily intended to protect Israeli civilians even if its mission is to ensure security for all. It stated: “The IDF’s [Israel Defense Forces] mission is to ensure the security of all residents of Judea and Samaria [West Bank], Palestinians and Israelis alike, and to operate to thwart terrorism and enforce law and order throughout Judea and Samaria to protect the security of Israeli civilians.” [319] The army’s spokesperson’s unit also affirmed that forces respond to settler attacks against Palestinians and their property, detaining suspects, when necessary, until the arrival of the police, and stated that: “Upon receiving any report regarding friction between Israelis and Palestinians or incidents involving an attack by an Israeli civilian, IDF forces are dispatched to the scene. In every incident involving friction or assault, IDF soldiers are expected to act to disperse those involved and restore order in the area, including in cases of violence or attempts to expel shepherds, and they handle irregular incidents in accordance with procedures”. [320] In parallel, since 1999, Israeli settlers set up at least seven unauthorized outposts with roads connecting directly to Kochav HaShahar, increasing Jewish presence and control of resources in the area. [469] By 2023, there were 10 outposts in the wider area surrounding Ein Samia; this number grew to 12 in 2026. Satellite imagery analysed by Amnesty International in October 2025 shows outposts to the north, south, west and east of Kochav HaShahar, with the closest located less than 1km from Ein Samia, sitting on the hillside overlooking the Palestinian community. Two more outposts surround Ein Samia on hills to the north and east, both less than 1.5km away, with the most recent one constructed in 2025. Satellite imagery clearly shows the expansion of most other outposts with new roads and structures appearing between 2023 and 2025. In December 2025, Israel’s security cabinet decided to legalize one of the outposts in the area as a new settlement, called Kochav HaShahar North, as part of a move to establish 19 new settlements in the West Bank. [470] Satellite imagery examined by Amnesty International showed that new land clearing at the Mizpe Kramim North outpost had already begun in April 2025, before the December 2025 decision to legalize Kochav Hashahar North. As of 8 February 2026, imagery shows over 10 new permanent looking structures and a hardened road. Based on the shifts visible in imagery, this is suspected to be the location of the new settlement, Kochav Hashahar North. Ein Samia spring and wells have long sustained farming in Al-Qabboun meadow and supplied water to 19 Palestinian communities. [471] The meadow, spanning 2-3km, has been essential to the agricultural self-sufficiency of several Palestinian communities in addition to Ein Samia, including the village of Kufr Malik. The report also concluded that inhuman/inhumane acts committed by Israel against Palestinians with the intent to maintain this system form part of a systematic and widespread attack directed against the Palestinian population and amount to the crime against humanity of apartheid. [664] In the OPT, this has involved forcible transfer, administrative detention, torture, unlawful killings and the denial of basic rights and freedoms, including through draconian movement restrictions. [665] Building on these findings, Amnesty International’s research and analysis determined that since the formation of the 37th government in December 2022 and throughout the period covered by this report, up to December 2025, Israel has committed serious violations of international human rights law and international humanitarian law in the context of an ethnic cleansing campaign targeting Palestinian Bedouin and herding communities in Area C. These violations include the war crime of unlawful deportation and transfer and the crime against humanity of deportation or forcible transfer of population. Although this report has focused on a three-year period, past reporting by Amnesty International has established that these violations and crimes were committed by Israel in the OPT in previous years. [666] The commission also described ethnic cleansing as a policy conducted to further a political doctrine through acts of violence designed “to instil terror in the civilian population” to “cause them to flee and never to return.” It also noted that the departure of a population before violent acts can take place is indicative of an ethnic cleansing policy and clarified that an ethnic cleansing campaign can be carried out by non-state actors. Amnesty International’s research shows that Israel’s government is pursuing a policy of ethnic cleansing of large parts of the West Bank, through the commission of war crimes and crimes against humanity both directly through its own forces and through support for violent attacks by settlers. Other organizations including UN bodies have reached similar conclusions. [684] The evidence presented in this report demonstrates that Israel has persisted in its policy of forcible transfer, which it has been committing as part of its unlawful occupation of the OPT and as a component of the crime against humanity of apartheid. These measures are not voluntary political actions; third states have legal obligations to ensure respect for international humanitarian law, [706] not render aid or assistance to Israel’s unlawful occupation and illegal settlements or to other serious violations, and to cooperate to bring Israel’s unlawful occupation to an end. Based on the shifts visible in imagery, this is suspected to be the location of the new settlement, Kochav Hashahar North.

Although this report has focused on a three-year period, past reporting by Amnesty International has established that these violations and crimes were committed by Israel in the OPT in previous years. [666]

The commission also described ethnic cleansing as a policy conducted to further a political doctrine through acts of violence designed “to instil terror in the civilian population” to “cause them to flee and never to return.” It also noted that the departure of a population before violent acts can take place is indicative of an ethnic cleansing policy and clarified that an ethnic cleansing campaign can be carried out by non-state actors.

The evidence presented in this report demonstrates that Israel has persisted in its policy of forcible transfer, which it has been committing as part of its unlawful occupation of the OPT and as a component of the crime against humanity of apartheid.

These measures are not voluntary political actions; third states have legal obligations to ensure respect for international humanitarian law, [706] not render aid or assistance to Israel’s unlawful occupation and illegal settlements or to other serious violations, and to cooperate to bring Israel’s unlawful occupation to an end. passages: Israel's security cabinet convened on Sunday for the first time since early October, holding a three-hour meeting amid concerns over a possible security escalation in the West Bank and preparations for a scenario in which Palestinian Authority security personnel turn their weapons against IDF soldiers and Israeli communities.
The cabinet meeting comes during a period of caretaker government, with Netanyahu and Gadi Eisenkot divided over whether significant security decisions should be made during this period.

extraction.body: Israel's security cabinet convened on Sunday for the first time since early October, holding a three-hour meeting amid concerns over a possible security escalation in the West Bank and preparations for a scenario in which Palestinian Authority security personnel turn their weapons against IDF soldiers and Israeli communities. The IDF's preparations focus on a scenario known as "turning the barrels," in which members of the Palestinian Authority's security services direct their weapons against IDF troops and Israeli communities. The discussion took place after plans developed by the IDF Central Command to address the scenario, which were originally scheduled to be presented to the cabinet in early October, were postponed following a change in the agenda. The IDF has formulated plans to respond to a possible attack by Palestinian security personnel, and the scenario has been rehearsed by the Judea and Samaria Division. IDF Chief of Staff Lt.-Gen. Eyal Zamir previously ordered additional troops to be deployed in the area and preparations to be made for the rapid mobilization of further units if necessary. Defense Minister Israel Katz raised the possibility in October of a large-scale confrontation with the Palestinian Authority, in which members of its security services and the Tanzim organization would act against IDF soldiers and Israeli settlers. According to Katz, Israel could declare war on the Palestinian Authority in such a scenario and launch an offensive in accordance with a plan prepared in advance. Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu also warned of the possibility during a tour of the security barrier along the seam line in Samaria. However, senior IDF officials emphasized in previous discussions that they had no intelligence indicating that Palestinian Authority security personnel intended to carry out such an attack. Central Command chief Maj.-Gen. Avi Bluth also warned that public discussion of the scenario could heighten tensions on the ground. In mid-October, Zamir announced that the IDF would reinforce its deployment in the West Bank , including the deployment of the 98th Division, and stressed the need to be prepared for a transition from defensive operations to offensive action. The IDF also warned of the possibility of an escalation following incidents of violence by Israeli extremists against Palestinians . The cabinet meeting comes during a period of caretaker government, with Netanyahu and Gadi Eisenkot divided over whether significant security decisions should be made during this period. sources.title: Security cabinet meets after six-week hiatus amid fears of West Bank escalation
passages: Israel's security cabinet convened on Sunday for the first time since early October, holding a three-hour meeting amid concerns over a possible security escalation in the West Bank and preparations for a scenario in which Palestinian Authority security personnel turn their weapons against IDF soldiers and Israeli communities.
The cabinet meeting comes during a period of caretaker government, with Netanyahu and Gadi Eisenkot divided over whether significant security decisions should be made during this period.

extraction.body: Israel's security cabinet convened on Sunday for the first time since early October, holding a three-hour meeting amid concerns over a possible security escalation in the West Bank and preparations for a scenario in which Palestinian Authority security personnel turn their weapons against IDF soldiers and Israeli communities. The IDF's preparations focus on a scenario known as "turning the barrels," in which members of the Palestinian Authority's security services direct their weapons against IDF troops and Israeli communities. The discussion took place after plans developed by the IDF Central Command to address the scenario, which were originally scheduled to be presented to the cabinet in early October, were postponed following a change in the agenda. The IDF has formulated plans to respond to a possible attack by Palestinian security personnel, and the scenario has been rehearsed by the Judea and Samaria Division. IDF Chief of Staff Lt.-Gen. Eyal Zamir previously ordered additional troops to be deployed in the area and preparations to be made for the rapid mobilization of further units if necessary. Defense Minister Israel Katz raised the possibility in October of a large-scale confrontation with the Palestinian Authority, in which members of its security services and the Tanzim organization would act against IDF soldiers and Israeli settlers. According to Katz, Israel could declare war on the Palestinian Authority in such a scenario and launch an offensive in accordance with a plan prepared in advance. Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu also warned of the possibility during a tour of the security barrier along the seam line in Samaria. However, senior IDF officials emphasized in previous discussions that they had no intelligence indicating that Palestinian Authority security personnel intended to carry out such an attack. Central Command chief Maj.-Gen. Avi Bluth also warned that public discussion of the scenario could heighten tensions on the ground. In mid-October, Zamir announced that the IDF would reinforce its deployment in the West Bank , including the deployment of the 98th Division, and stressed the need to be prepared for a transition from defensive operations to offensive action. The IDF also warned of the possibility of an escalation following incidents of violence by Israeli extremists against Palestinians . The cabinet meeting comes during a period of caretaker government, with Netanyahu and Gadi Eisenkot divided over whether significant security decisions should be made during this period. extraction.body: Michael Saylor, the executive chairman of Strategy Inc. ( NASDAQ: MSTR | MSTR Price Prediction ), shared his purchase chart on X on November 1, 2026. This move often signals that another Bitcoin ( CRYPTO: BTC ) buy is coming. This hint comes just 10 days before MSCI’s decision on whether to include Strategy Inc. in its global stock indexes. On November 11, MSCI ( NYSE: MSCI ) will announce its final list of companies that are exiting its indexes, and previous simulations indicated that Strategy Inc. might be on that list. Strategy Inc. held 848,517 BTC valued at around $66 billion as of October 25. However, this year, the company sold about $432 million worth of Bitcoin to cover preferred dividends and repurchase STRC preferred stock. Saylor said in comments reported on October 31 that the company can raise up to $30 billion in “digital credit,” which refers to its preferred stock, to finance additional purchases. Michael Burry Betting GameStop (GME) Will Level Up The company’s stock has been under pressure, falling faster than its Bitcoin holdings. On October 30, MSTR closed at approximately $131, down 7.8% for the day and 14.8% over the past month. Meanwhile, Bitcoin trades at $78,050 as of November 1, up 0.7% over 24 hours but down 7.8% over 30 days. While Strategy Inc. still sells analytics software under the MicroStrategy brand, its third-quarter (Q3) results show this segment is relatively small. Software revenue dipped 2.5% from the previous year to $125 million, missing the $129 million forecast. Strategy Inc.’s main profits come from Bitcoin. The company values its holdings at current market prices, and a $20.9 billion gain from Bitcoin contributed significantly, boosting Q3 net income to $19.5 billion after net losses of $12.5 billion in Q1 and $8.2 billion in Q2. To fund its Bitcoin purchases, Strategy Inc. has raised $21.2 billion this year and spent $14.3 billion on Bitcoin. Currently, it has $16 billion in preferred stock outstanding, with the main issue (STRC) offering a 12% annual dividend but trading below the $100 face value the company aims to restore. Dividends have become a significant financial burden, rising to $420 million in Q3 from $140 million a year earlier. The company holds $5.1 billion in cash-like assets, which management states will cover dividends and interest for 3.4 years. However, the BTC Yield, which tracks the amount of Bitcoin backing each share, is negative 3.7% this year, indicating each share now holds less Bitcoin than it did at the beginning of the year. Saylor’s posts are just indications of a possible purchase; the actual size and funding are revealed in the 8-K report that Strategy Inc. submits to the SEC afterward. The previous report, released in mid-October, indicated a purchase of just 250 Bitcoin. Funding remains a crucial challenge. Saylor mentioned in February that Strategy Inc. doesn’t sell MSTR when the stock is weak or when STRC trades below $100 . Since MSTR has declined by 48.7% over the past year and STRC is below $100, these funding routes appear limited, making the $30 billion figure more of an upper limit than a guarantee. An MSCI exit wouldn’t automatically require the company to sell its Bitcoin. In that scenario, selling Bitcoin could become necessary to cover dividend payments . For Bitcoin, the bigger concern is losing a consistent buyer. Strategy Inc. financed a significant portion of its $14.3 billion Bitcoin purchases this year by selling stock. A weakened stock price could hinder its ability to raise funds. Bitcoin is currently trading near $67,200 after a fresh leg down that briefly took it to about $66,580. The swing has been brutal because just about a month ago, Bitcoin.com News reported that Saylor’s firm was still $5 billion up on its bitcoin even after MSCI news knocked MSTR shares down nearly 10%. Saturday’s drop came fast after analysts reported over $330 million in liquidations across the crypto market in two hours. During that stretch, BTC fell under $67,000, ether under $1,900 and XRP under $1. Popular chartists noted that bitcoin had once again entered a bear market after falling more than 20% from its September high. To this point, BTC is down about 11.6% over seven days and 17% over 30 days, and it now sits roughly 47% below its October 2025 all-time high of $126,080. The Crypto Fear and Greed Index printed a reading of 13 , or “Extreme Fear,” on Friday night. Strategy kept buying into the slide, and its Nov. 9 filing showed that the firm had added 1,036 BTC at an average of $79,012, funded with MSTR stock sales. Those coins alone are now about 15% underwater. MSTR closed Friday at $111.62 , down about 22% from its $142.54 close on Nov. 4. The slide followed MSCI’s decision this week to drop the company from its indexes, which Bitcoin.com News covered when Strategy lost its MSCI spot . Strategy CEO Phong Le pushed back on the index fears in a CNBC interview yesterday, saying only about 3% of Strategy’s shares are tied to MSCI indexes and he expects little impact from the exclusion. Adding to the sting, MSCI said UK-based bitcoin treasury firm The Smarter Web Company will join its Micro Cap Index effective Nov. 30. Critics have zeroed in on the payouts, and Peter Schiff recently questioned Strategy’s 12% yield on its preferred stock as bitcoin fell. The company’s filing offers some context as Strategy reported a U.S. dollar (USD) Reserve of $4.77 billion (as of Nov. 8), set aside for preferred dividends and debt interest, and said it used $21.1 million of that reserve for dividends during the prior week. Being underwater on paper does not by itself force Strategy to sell anything, and its USD Reserve exists so dividends don’t depend on selling BTC. Still, the gap can have a direct impact on sentiment. extraction.body: Michael Saylor’s Strategy is currently sitting on a paper loss of more than $7 billion on its 850,364 BTC stash. This happened after bitcoin slid below $67,000 earlier today. The world’s largest corporate bitcoin holder is now officially in the red, with Strategy’s most recent 8-K filing with the SEC showing that the company held 850,364 BTC as of Nov. 9, bought for an aggregate $64.16 billion (at an average purchase price of $75,456 per coin, fees included). Bitcoin is currently trading near $67,200 after a fresh leg down that briefly took it to about $66,580. At that price, Strategy’s holdings were worth roughly $56.9 billion, leaving an unrealized loss of about $7.2 billion. The swing has been brutal because just about a month ago, Bitcoin.com News reported that Saylor’s firm was still $5 billion up on its bitcoin even after MSCI news knocked MSTR shares down nearly 10%. Saturday’s drop came fast after analysts reported over $330 million in liquidations across the crypto market in two hours. During that stretch, BTC fell under $67,000, ether under $1,900 and XRP under $1. Popular chartists noted that bitcoin had once again entered a bear market after falling more than 20% from its September high. To this point, BTC is down about 11.6% over seven days and 17% over 30 days, and it now sits roughly 47% below its October 2025 all-time high of $126,080. The Crypto Fear and Greed Index printed a reading of 13 , or “Extreme Fear,” on Friday night. Strategy kept buying into the slide, and its Nov. 9 filing showed that the firm had added 1,036 BTC at an average of $79,012, funded with MSTR stock sales. Those coins alone are now about 15% underwater. MSTR closed Friday at $111.62 , down about 22% from its $142.54 close on Nov. 4. The slide followed MSCI’s decision this week to drop the company from its indexes, which Bitcoin.com News covered when Strategy lost its MSCI spot . Strategy CEO Phong Le pushed back on the index fears in a CNBC interview yesterday, saying only about 3% of Strategy’s shares are tied to MSCI indexes and he expects little impact from the exclusion. Adding to the sting, MSCI said UK-based bitcoin treasury firm The Smarter Web Company will join its Micro Cap Index effective Nov. 30. facts.text: Michael Saylor's bitcoin vehicle is under pressure from two sides at once: an index provider is dropping it, and the coin it holds keeps falling.
Index selling happens once and then stops, and some of it may already be priced in.
Saylor says bitcoin is entering its next bull market.

Strategy pairs a legacy MicroStrategy analytics software business with the largest corporate treasury of Bitcoin (CRYPTO:BTC).
Strategy had previously estimated that removal could cause about $2.8 billion in selling.

Sam has written about crypto professionally since 2019 and has published more than 2,000 articles.
His analysis is syndicated on Yahoo Finance, MSN and AOL and has been cited by other crypto news sites.
He also founded MacLabs Marketing, a content and personal branding agency for crypto founders and executives.

An MSCI exit wouldn’t automatically require the company to sell its Bitcoin.

For Bitcoin, the bigger concern is losing a consistent buyer.

Some institutional voices still prefer Bitcoin within crypto.
Speaking on the Unchained podcast, Bitwise's chief investment officer said "Bitcoin is a more steady position" for institutional capital.
Bitcoin can still deliver sharp rallies, but how much an investor makes depends heavily on when they buy.
Someone who bought near the late-2021 high has close to nothing to show for five years, while SPY rewarded buyers at nearly any entry point over the same period.
Yahoo Finance is not a broker-dealer or investment adviser and does not offer securities or cryptocurrencies for sale or facilitate trading.
SPY crushed Bitcoin over five years, gaining 61% on price alone while Bitcoin managed just 7%, turning $10,000 into $16,144 versus $10,740.
Which should an investor saving for retirement own right now: Bitcoin (CRYPTO:BTC) or the State Street SPDR S&P 500 ETF Trust ( NYSEARCA:SPY )?
Bitcoin is known for making wealth, but the matched five-year numbers favor the plain index fund by a wide margin.
Over nearly the same window, SPY rose from $467.27 on November 12, 2021 to $754.37 on November 13, 2026, a price gain of 61.44%.
Over ten years, SPY's price gain comes to 245.6%.
Bitcoin pays no dividends, so its return depends entirely on what the next buyer will pay.
SPY passes along dividends from its underlying companies.
With those dividends reinvested, SPY's five-year total return was about 72.6%, which would have grown $10,000 to roughly $17,260.
The fund charges an expense ratio of 0.0945%.
For retirees who draw income from their portfolios, a cash payout makes a real difference.

A loss on Bitcoin's scale takes years to recover from, and a retiree selling assets to cover living costs may never get those years (that early-withdrawal damage is exactly what planners call sequence-of-returns risk, and we walked through how to protect against it in a free guide here).
Bitcoin lost 20.43% over 30 days and now trades below its 20-day, 50-day and 200-day moving averages.
Over roughly the same month, SPY slipped just 1.98%.
The VIX, Wall Street's fear gauge, stands at 18.70, inside its normal range.
SPY also spreads its risk across about 500 major U.S. companies.
Its largest holding, NVIDIA ( NASDAQ:NVDA ), makes up only 7.58% of assets.
Bitcoin trades at $64,868, which is 48.55% below its all-time high of $126,080, set on October 6, 2025.
Year to date, Bitcoin is down 25.93%, while SPY is up 10.62%.
SPY wins on all three measures: long-term returns, income, and risk.
For a retirement investor, the data points to SPY as the steadier option.
Bitcoin's upside appeals only to investors who can afford to lose a large share of what they put in and who don't need the money for a decade.

passages: It was the resignation heard across the world.
Jensen Huang, Nvidia’s embattled CEO who co-founded and led the company for 33 years, had officially stepped down .
“It’s like a bomb went off,” one neocloud founder told TechCrunch when he first heard the news.
Most of the significant decisions to invest in startups often came from Jensen himself, according to Umesh Padval, managing partner at Seligman Ventures.

Huang’s absence leaves the startup ecosystem without one of its biggest champions and with far less capital for now, investors say, which could have a massive impact on dealmaking, valuations, funding, and even competition.

If the company does grow more conservative with its startup investments, that could leave more room for rivals and smaller competitors. (Coincidentally, Google announced two new chips this week amid Huang’s Nvidia fallout.)
“When Nvidia was on the cap table, everyone felt safe,” Padval said.
Without that backing, investors say traditional VCs are likely to think twice before writing checks into these startups and may even pause certain dealmaking.
“Jensen’s initiatives are a big reason an ecosystem has emerged despite that,” Zain Javaid, founder of the hardware company Ghost, said.
Some investors with whom TechCrunch spoke hope that large cloud companies and other chipmakers will step in to back startups and fill some of the void that will likely be left by Huang.

extraction.body: It was the resignation heard across the world. Jensen Huang, Nvidia’s embattled CEO who co-founded and led the company for 33 years, had officially stepped down . “It’s like a bomb went off,” one neocloud founder told TechCrunch when he first heard the news. Over the last several years, Nvidia has been a prolific investor , pouring tens of billions into startups annually and participating in 105 rounds this year alone, often as the largest investor, according to PitchBook. “If that direction changes, it’ll be a big blow to so many young companies,” said Maria Davidson, founder of Relational Capital. Huang’s absence leaves the startup ecosystem without one of its biggest champions and with far less capital for now, investors say, which could have a massive impact on dealmaking, valuations, funding, and even competition. “Nvidia is carrying almost every AI-native startup from application to neocloud,” Dawn Capital’s Shamillah Bankiya told TechCrunch. Most of the significant decisions to invest in startups often came from Jensen himself, according to Umesh Padval, managing partner at Seligman Ventures. Padval has known Huang since serving on the board of Mellanox Technologies, a networking chipmaker Nvidia acquired for approximately $7 billion in 2020. While there is hope that Huang’s eventual successor will resume his dealmaking spree, investors aren’t hopeful that it will happen in the short term. Nvidia’s interim CEO, Colette Kress, is expected to institute some changes , especially when it comes to Nvidia’s investments into AI startups at the crux of the billion-dollar data center build-out . Huang’s rampant dealmaking in this sphere has been a source of concern for Wall Street. “She’s much more conservative,” one investor said of Kress. “I don’t think she’s going to commit the same amount of money to keep the early-stage ecosystem going.” Nvidia’s biggest bets were backing neoclouds, inference providers, and open weight models, which are expensive for smaller companies to build. “Jensen’s initiatives are a big reason an ecosystem has emerged despite that,” Zain Javaid, founder of the hardware company Ghost, said. For instance, Nvidia backed CoreWeave when it was still private and participated in two of Crusoe’s rounds, including its $1.4 billion Series E. It bought Hugging Face this year for $13 billion (expected to close in 2027) and holds investments in Mistral AI, Lambda, and Black Forest Labs. Nvidia was often the largest investor in the deals. Last year, it wrote an $800 million check into a $2 billion Series B round for Reflection AI, before the open source startup began to earn meaningful revenue, according to the Wall Street Journal . “Jensen believed in open source and frankly speaking, Europe,” Bankiya said of how Huang invested so much in AI across the world. The cease of that support in other regions outside of America, like Europe “would be a massive funding and honestly ecosystem gap that no one can fill.” It’s also true that Nvidia was such a dominant player in the ecosystem that at times, it felt like a monopoly. By backing so many companies with such generous checks, Nvidia effectively locked those startups into using its chips, which helped reinforce its dominant market position. If the company does grow more conservative with its startup investments, that could leave more room for rivals and smaller competitors. (Coincidentally, Google announced two new chips this week amid Huang’s Nvidia fallout.) Some investors with whom TechCrunch spoke hope that large cloud companies and other chipmakers will step in to back startups and fill some of the void that will likely be left by Huang. Dharmesh Thakker, a general partner at Battery Ventures, for example, expects Big Tech rivals to vie for Nvidia’s investment crown, “depending upon who brings the best combination of a great product, an ecosystem and community to compete with CUDA, and the financial power to bankroll the ecosystem,” he said. CUDA is Nvidia’s software platform that enables developers to run AI models on its GPUs. While companies like Google, Amazon, Microsoft, and AMD may back mature startups to drive adoption of their chips and clouds, Thakker doubts they will pour hundreds of millions into pre-revenue infrastructure startups the way Nvidia did. Under Huang, infrastructure companies that needed $100 million to $500 million in GPUs would often raise half of that amount at valuations of $1 billion or more from Nvidia just to get started, one VC said. The chipmaker’s participation gave other investors the comfort in backing these companies at the lofty valuations. Now Nvidia is expected to be more selective in the new companies it backs, while writing smaller-sized checks into its existing portfolio, contributing to a drop in valuations. “When Nvidia was on the cap table, everyone felt safe,” Padval said. Without that backing, investors say traditional VCs are likely to think twice before writing checks into these startups and may even pause certain dealmaking. Even so, few believe that Nvidia’s investment slowdown will by itself halt the broader AI boom. Though everyone agrees that Huang is a massive loss for Nvidia, one of his ex-employees, Amulya Vishwanath, who now runs her own VC fund, said that “founders and leaders must be held accountable,” and that the ecosystem is bigger than one person. “That talent will, and must, continue to thrive.” Dominic-Madori Davis is a senior venture capital and startup reporter at TechCrunch. She is based in New York City. You can contact or verify outreach from Dominic by emailing [email protected] or via encrypted message at +1 646 831-7565 on Signal. Over the last several years, Nvidia has been a prolific investor , pouring tens of billions into startups annually and participating in 105 rounds this year alone, often as the largest investor, according to PitchBook. "If that direction changes, it'll be a big blow to so many young companies," said Maria Davidson, founder of Relational Capital. Huang's absence leaves the startup ecosystem without one of its biggest champions and with far less capital for now, investors say, which could have a massive impact on dealmaking, valuations, funding, and even competition. "Nvidia is carrying almost every AI-native startup from application to neocloud," Dawn Capital's Shamillah Bankiya told TechCrunch. Most of the significant decisions to invest in startups often came from Jensen himself, according to Umesh Padval, managing partner at Seligman Ventures. Padval has known Huang since serving on the board of Mellanox Technologies, a networking chipmaker Nvidia acquired for approximately $7 billion in 2020. While there is hope that Huang's eventual successor will resume his dealmaking spree, investors aren't hopeful that it will happen in the short term. Nvidia's interim CEO, Colette Kress, is expected to institute some changes , especially when it comes to Nvidia's investments into AI startups at the crux of the billion-dollar data center build-out . Huang's rampant dealmaking in this sphere has been a source of concern for Wall Street. "She's much more conservative," one investor said of Kress. "I don't think she's going to commit the same amount of money to keep the early-stage ecosystem going." Nvidia's biggest bets were backing neoclouds, inference providers, and open weight models, which are expensive for smaller companies to build. "Jensen's initiatives are a big reason an ecosystem has emerged despite that," Zain Javaid, founder of the hardware company Ghost, said. For instance, Nvidia backed CoreWeave when it was still private and participated in two of Crusoe's rounds, including its $1.4 billion Series E. It bought Hugging Face this year for $13 billion (expected to close in 2027) and holds investments in Mistral AI, Lambda, and Black Forest Labs. Nvidia was often the largest investor in the deals. Last year, it wrote an $800 million check into a $2 billion Series B round for Reflection AI, before the open source startup began to earn meaningful revenue, according to the Wall Street Journal . "Jensen believed in open source and frankly speaking, Europe," Bankiya said of how Huang invested so much in AI across the world. The cease of that support in other regions outside of America, like Europe "would be a massive funding and honestly ecosystem gap that no one can fill." It's also true that Nvidia was such a dominant player in the ecosystem that at times, it felt like a monopoly. By backing so many companies with such generous checks, Nvidia effectively locked those startups into using its chips, which helped reinforce its dominant market position. If the company does grow more conservative with its startup investments, that could leave more room for rivals and smaller competitors. (Coincidentally, Google announced two new chips this week amid Huang's Nvidia fallout.) Some investors with whom TechCrunch spoke hope that large cloud companies and other chipmakers will step in to back startups and fill some of the void that will likely be left by Huang. Dharmesh Thakker, a general partner at Battery Ventures, for example, expects Big Tech rivals to vie for Nvidia's investment crown, "depending upon who brings the best combination of a great product, an ecosystem and community to compete with CUDA, and the financial power to bankroll the ecosystem," he said. CUDA is Nvidia's software platform that enables developers to run AI models on its GPUs. While companies like Google, Amazon, Microsoft, and AMD may back mature startups to drive adoption of their chips and clouds, Thakker doubts they will pour hundreds of millions into pre-revenue infrastructure startups the way Nvidia did. Under Huang, infrastructure companies that needed $100 million to $500 million in GPUs would often raise half of that amount at valuations of $1 billion or more from Nvidia just to get started, one VC said. The chipmaker's participation gave other investors the comfort in backing these companies at the lofty valuations. Now Nvidia is expected to be more selective in the new companies it backs, while writing smaller-sized checks into its existing portfolio, contributing to a drop in valuations. "When Nvidia was on the cap table, everyone felt safe," Padval said. Without that backing, investors say traditional VCs are likely to think twice before writing checks into these startups and may even pause certain dealmaking. Even so, few believe that Nvidia's investment slowdown will by itself halt the broader AI boom. Though everyone agrees that Huang is a massive loss for Nvidia, one of his ex-employees, Amulya Vishwanath, who now runs her own VC fund, said that "founders and leaders must be held accountable," and that the ecosystem is bigger than one person. "That talent will, and must, continue to thrive."

passages: It was the resignation heard across the world. Jensen Huang, Nvidia’s embattled CEO who co-founded and led the company for 33 years, had officially stepped down . “It’s like a bomb went off,” one neocloud founder told TechCrunch when he first heard the news.

Over the last several years, Nvidia has been a prolific investor , pouring tens of billions into startups annually and participating in 105 rounds this year alone, often as the largest investor, according to PitchBook. “If that direction changes, it’ll be a big blow to so many young companies,” said Maria Davidson, founder of Relational Capital.

Huang’s absence leaves the startup ecosystem without one of its biggest champions and with far less capital for now, investors say, which could have a massive impact on dealmaking, valuations, funding, and even competition.
“Nvidia is carrying almost every AI-native startup from application to neocloud,” Dawn Capital’s Shamillah Bankiya told TechCrunch.

Most of the significant decisions to invest in startups often came from Jensen himself, according to Umesh Padval, managing partner at Seligman Ventures. Padval has known Huang since serving on the board of Mellanox Technologies, a networking chipmaker Nvidia acquired for approximately $7 billion in 2020. While there is hope that Huang’s eventual successor will resume his dealmaking spree, investors aren’t hopeful that it will happen in the short term.

Nvidia’s interim CEO, Colette Kress, is expected to institute some changes , especially when it comes to Nvidia’s investments into AI startups at the crux of the billion-dollar data center build-out . Huang’s rampant dealmaking in this sphere has been a source of concern for Wall Street.
“She’s much more conservative,” one investor said of Kress. “I don’t think she’s going to commit the same amount of money to keep the early-stage ecosystem going.”

Nvidia’s biggest bets were backing neoclouds, inference providers, and open weight models, which are expensive for smaller companies to build. “Jensen’s initiatives are a big reason an ecosystem has emerged despite that,” Zain Javaid, founder of the hardware company Ghost, said.

For instance, Nvidia backed CoreWeave when it was still private and participated in two of Crusoe’s rounds, including its $1.4 billion Series E. It bought Hugging Face this year for $13 billion (expected to close in 2027) and holds investments in Mistral AI, Lambda, and Black Forest Labs. Nvidia was often the largest investor in the deals. Last year, it wrote an $800 million check into a $2 billion Series B round for Reflection AI, before the open source startup began to earn meaningful revenue, according to the Wall Street Journal .

“Jensen believed in open source and frankly speaking, Europe,” Bankiya said of how Huang invested so much in AI across the world. The cease of that support in other regions outside of America, like Europe “would be a massive funding and honestly ecosystem gap that no one can fill.”

It’s also true that Nvidia was such a dominant player in the ecosystem that at times, it felt like a monopoly. By backing so many companies with such generous checks, Nvidia effectively locked those startups into using its chips, which helped reinforce its dominant market position.

If the company does grow more conservative with its startup investments, that could leave more room for rivals and smaller competitors. (Coincidentally, Google announced two new chips this week amid Huang’s Nvidia fallout.)
Some investors with whom TechCrunch spoke hope that large cloud companies and other chipmakers will step in to back startups and fill some of the void that will likely be left by Huang.

Dharmesh Thakker, a general partner at Battery Ventures, for example, expects Big Tech rivals to vie for Nvidia’s investment crown, “depending upon who brings the best combination of a great product, an ecosystem and community to compete with CUDA, and the financial power to bankroll the ecosystem,” he said. CUDA is Nvidia’s software platform that enables developers to run AI models on its GPUs.

While companies like Google, Amazon, Microsoft, and AMD may back mature startups to drive adoption of their chips and clouds, Thakker doubts they will pour hundreds of millions into pre-revenue infrastructure startups the way Nvidia did.

Under Huang, infrastructure companies that needed $100 million to $500 million in GPUs would often raise half of that amount at valuations of $1 billion or more from Nvidia just to get started, one VC said. The chipmaker’s participation gave other investors the comfort in backing these companies at the lofty valuations.
Now Nvidia is expected to be more selective in the new companies it backs, while writing smaller-sized checks into its existing portfolio, contributing to a drop in valuations.

“When Nvidia was on the cap table, everyone felt safe,” Padval said. Without that backing, investors say traditional VCs are likely to think twice before writing checks into these startups and may even pause certain dealmaking.
Even so, few believe that Nvidia’s investment slowdown will by itself halt the broader AI boom.

Though everyone agrees that Huang is a massive loss for Nvidia, one of his ex-employees, Amulya Vishwanath, who now runs her own VC fund, said that “founders and leaders must be held accountable,” and that the ecosystem is bigger than one person. “That talent will, and must, continue to thrive.”
Dominic-Madori Davis is a senior venture capital and startup reporter at TechCrunch. She is based in New York City.

Sellers hold control: Bitcoin trades below its 20-, 50- and 200-day averages, and spot ETFs bled 21% of their net assets since October 21. Past crashes took nine months to nearly three years to recover, and the Fed's rate hikes echo the 28-month slog after 2022. It sounds nuts, but SoFi is giving new Active Invest users up to $1,000 in stock for a limited time, and all it takes is a $50 deposit to get started. See for yourself (Sponsor) Bitcoin (CRYPTO: BTC) needs to rise about 95% to reach its all-time high of $126,080, which was set on October 6, 2025. Currently priced at $64,664, Bitcoin is 48.7% below that peak and has dropped 26.1% since the beginning of 2026. Sellers are still active in the market. On November 14, Bitcoin closed at $64,120, marking the lowest point in a 30-day trading range, which peaked at $84,082 on October 21, a significant 23.7% drop. It has also fallen below its 200-week moving average, a key gauge of long-term price trends. So, when can we expect Bitcoin to bounce back to its all-time high, and what factors could delay this recovery? With approximately 20.1 million Bitcoins in circulation, achieving a price of $126,080 would mean a market value of around $2.5 trillion. This is nearly double the current market cap of $1.3 trillion. However, increasing supply complicates Bitcoin's path to recovery. Miners continue to produce new coins, so maintaining the same price requires more investment. For example, Bitcoin closed at $64,654 on November 13, 2021, with a market cap of about $1.22 trillion. Now, at a similar price of $64,664, its market value has risen to approximately $1.30 trillion. Moreover, market trends indicate downward momentum. Bitcoin is currently trading below its 20-day average of $75,828, its 50-day average of $80,159, and its 200-day average of $72,982, which are 17.3%, 24%, and 12.9% higher than its current price, respectively. Spot Bitcoin ETFs, which hold the coin for stock market investors, saw outflows every trading day from November 5 to 13, according to SoSoValue, leading to a 21.1% drop in their net assets from $109.3 billion on October 21 to $86.2 billion. Bitcoin has experienced significant drops before, and recovery times have varied considerably, often tied to Federal Reserve actions. Our review of the last three major Bitcoin crashes found these recovery times. 2018 bear market. Bitcoin plummeted 84% from $20,000 in December 2017 to $3,200 in December 2018, taking nearly three years to reclaim the $20,000 mark. 2020 COVID crash. A 58% decline quickly reversed after the Fed injected over $4 trillion into the economy. Bitcoin surpassed its 2017 high by December 2020, about nine months after hitting its lowest point. 2022 collapse. After a 77% drop from $69,000 in November 2021, as the Fed raised rates by 525 basis points, Bitcoin took 28 months to reach a new all-time high in March 2024. Currently, the situation resembles the 2022 collapse due to the Fed's ongoing rate hikes. With the target rate rising to 4% on September 16 and another meeting scheduled for December 9, Bitcoin may face another lengthy recovery. A similar 28-month wait from the October 2025 peak could see Bitcoin hit new highs around early 2028. Despite the downturn, several analysts still predict higher Bitcoin prices, though most of these calls came before the latest slide. Bernstein. A research note from August projected Bitcoin reaching $125,000 by December 31 and $150,000 by mid-2027, connecting these targets to Bitcoin's four-year cycle following each halving. Alex Thorn. Galaxy's head of research maintained his $250,000 target by the end of 2027, calling a return to around $125,000 "pretty conservative." Standard Chartered. The bank revised its expectations but still anticipates Bitcoin could hit $500,000 by 2030. ARK Invest. The firm forecasts a central price of $710,000 by 2030, with an optimistic estimate reaching as high as $1.5 million. Bitcoin also appears to have less distance to cover than other major cryptocurrencies. Our September analysis of which coin gets back first suggested Bitcoin could rebound more quickly, needing only a 49% rise. sources.title: Nvidia privately confirmed it could track chips to fight smuggling, even as industry publicly questioned feasibility - MIT Technology Review
passages: Representatives from Nvidia told Illinois representative Bill Foster that it would be technically possible to implement the anti-smuggling measures called for in the Chip Security Act, Foster told MIT Technology Review in an interview on Thursday, even while an industry group claimed they were “potentially infeasible.”

It declined to answer directly, instead sending a statement: “Governments and media have found insignificant diversion of controlled US products—a drop in the bucket compared to the ocean of domestic compute China already has.”

In March 2026, the Semiconductor Industry Association, of which Nvidia is a member, explicitly opposed the bill and wrote that its mandates for chip tracking were “new, untested, and potentially infeasible.”
Other technology Nvidia has built for its customers suggests that the company can indeed offer accurate tracking of its chips’ locations.
In December 2025, for example, it announced a new tool called Fleet Intelligence that would allow customers to monitor how its advanced chips were performing across different data center locations.
In doing so, the tool could indicate which country chips were in, Nvidia confirmed to Reuters, but the company would not elaborate on whether this technology could be used to prevent smuggling.

But if the requirements of the bill pass as part of the Senate’s National Defense Authorization Act, the new tracking mechanisms would only tell investigators where the chips are, not offer a way to disconnect them if it’s revealed they have been smuggled.
The new rule would require licenses to operate advanced GPUs, and before a GPU could connect, its valid license would need to be verified.
The recent fallout at Nvidia involves a number of people and companies alleged to be involved in chip smuggling.
Alice Huang, with whom Jensen Huang reportedly had an affair, runs Megaspeed, a Singaporean firm now under investigation for smuggling advanced GPUs to China.
A US Commerce Department inquiry into the company was reportedly halted after invention by Nvidia.
Megaspeed reportedly bought chips from Supermicro, a company that packages Nvidia’s chips onto servers.
Foster said he did not ask Nvidia’s representatives why they weren’t voluntarily adopting such chip-tracking tools if they could technically do so.

Foster, a Democrat who serves on the Committee on Science, Space, and Technology, is a cosponsor of the act, which would introduce geotracking requirements to verify the location of advanced AI chips in order to prevent their smuggling to China.

“They never put anything in writing,” Foster says, but during technical discussions on the possibility of such safeguards, their reaction was “yeah, of course we can do this.” This private acknowledgment to Foster goes further than anything Nvidia has previously made public.
Nvidia did not respond to requests for comment or confirmation of Foster’s characterization.

When the Chip Security Act was introduced, in May 2025, lawmakers said the technology to implement it existed, something Nvidia has not publicly confirmed. In March 2026, the Semiconductor Industry Association, of which Nvidia is a member, explicitly opposed the bill and wrote that its mandates for chip tracking were “new, untested, and potentially infeasible.” But privately, Nvidia representatives working with Foster told the lawmaker that the company could implement them. “They never put anything in writing,” Foster says, but during technical discussions on the possibility of such safeguards, their reaction was “yeah, of course we can do this.” This private acknowledgment to Foster goes further than anything Nvidia has previously made public. Other technology Nvidia has built for its customers suggests that the company can indeed offer accurate tracking of its chips’ locations. In December 2025, for example, it announced a new tool called Fleet Intelligence that would allow customers to monitor how its advanced chips were performing across different data center locations. In doing so, the tool could indicate which country chips were in, Nvidia confirmed to Reuters, but the company would not elaborate on whether this technology could be used to prevent smuggling. Nvidia did not respond to requests for comment or confirmation of Foster’s characterization. In early October, when lawmakers were reportedly increasingly concerned about Nvidia’s role in smuggling, MIT Technology Review asked the company if Fleet Intelligence could be used to prevent the practice. It declined to answer directly, instead sending a statement: “Governments and media have found insignificant diversion of controlled US products—a drop in the bucket compared to the ocean of domestic compute China already has.” The recent fallout at Nvidia involves a number of people and companies alleged to be involved in chip smuggling. Alice Huang, with whom Jensen Huang reportedly had an affair, runs Megaspeed, a Singaporean firm now under investigation for smuggling advanced GPUs to China. A US Commerce Department inquiry into the company was reportedly halted after invention by Nvidia. Megaspeed reportedly bought chips from Supermicro, a company that packages Nvidia’s chips onto servers. The Chip Security Act as drafted would require a mechanism to track the locations of chips, either by inspections of facilities, attestations by companies, or ping-based location mechanisms. The ping-based technique, the hardest option to circumvent, would require the GPU to send a signal of its location when it comes online. In September, the Center for Security and Emerging Technology found it would be the most cost-effective option. Foster said he did not ask Nvidia’s representatives why they weren’t voluntarily adopting such chip-tracking tools if they could technically do so. But if the requirements of the bill pass as part of the Senate’s National Defense Authorization Act, the new tracking mechanisms would only tell investigators where the chips are, not offer a way to disconnect them if it’s revealed they have been smuggled. Foster told MIT Technology Review he intends to introduce new, stricter legislation in the new year that would offer a workaround. The new rule would require licenses to operate advanced GPUs, and before a GPU could connect, its valid license would need to be verified. passages: The Chip Security Act is getting renewed attention following Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s resignation and reported affair with an alleged Chinese spy.

Representatives from Nvidia told Illinois representative Bill Foster that it would be technically possible to implement the anti-smuggling measures called for in the Chip Security Act, Foster told MIT Technology Review in an interview on Thursday, even while an industry group claimed they were “potentially infeasible.”

Foster, a Democrat who serves on the Committee on Science, Space, and Technology, is a cosponsor of the act, which would introduce geotracking requirements to verify the location of advanced AI chips in order to prevent their smuggling to China. It is one of three chip-security bills under consideration for inclusion in the Senate’s National Defense Authorization Act, each of which is drawing renewed attention after Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s resignation and reported affair with an alleged Chinese spy.

When the Chip Security Act was introduced, in May 2025, lawmakers said the technology to implement it existed, something Nvidia has not publicly confirmed. In March 2026, the Semiconductor Industry Association, of which Nvidia is a member, explicitly opposed the bill and wrote that its mandates for chip tracking were “new, untested, and potentially infeasible.”
But privately, Nvidia representatives working with Foster told the lawmaker that the company could implement them.

“They never put anything in writing,” Foster says, but during technical discussions on the possibility of such safeguards, their reaction was “yeah, of course we can do this.” This private acknowledgment to Foster goes further than anything Nvidia has previously made public.

Other technology Nvidia has built for its customers suggests that the company can indeed offer accurate tracking of its chips’ locations. In December 2025, for example, it announced a new tool called Fleet Intelligence that would allow customers to monitor how its advanced chips were performing across different data center locations. In doing so, the tool could indicate which country chips were in, Nvidia confirmed to Reuters, but the company would not elaborate on whether this technology could be used to prevent smuggling.
Nvidia did not respond to requests for comment or confirmation of Foster’s characterization.

In early October, when lawmakers were reportedly increasingly concerned about Nvidia’s role in smuggling, MIT Technology Review asked the company if Fleet Intelligence could be used to prevent the practice. It declined to answer directly, instead sending a statement: “Governments and media have found insignificant diversion of controlled US products—a drop in the bucket compared to the ocean of domestic compute China already has.”

The recent fallout at Nvidia involves a number of people and companies alleged to be involved in chip smuggling. Alice Huang, with whom Jensen Huang reportedly had an affair, runs Megaspeed, a Singaporean firm now under investigation for smuggling advanced GPUs to China. A US Commerce Department inquiry into the company was reportedly halted after invention by Nvidia. Megaspeed reportedly bought chips from Supermicro, a company that packages Nvidia’s chips onto servers.

The Chip Security Act as drafted would require a mechanism to track the locations of chips, either by inspections of facilities, attestations by companies, or ping-based location mechanisms. The ping-based technique, the hardest option to circumvent, would require the GPU to send a signal of its location when it comes online. In September, the Center for Security and Emerging Technology found it would be the most cost-effective option.
Foster said he did not ask Nvidia’s representatives why they weren’t voluntarily adopting such chip-tracking tools if they could technically do so.

But if the requirements of the bill pass as part of the Senate’s National Defense Authorization Act, the new tracking mechanisms would only tell investigators where the chips are, not offer a way to disconnect them if it’s revealed they have been smuggled. Foster told MIT Technology Review he intends to introduce new, stricter legislation in the new year that would offer a workaround. The new rule would require licenses to operate advanced GPUs, and before a GPU could connect, its valid license would need to be verified.

In the meantime, the controversy at Nvidia, Foster says, has fueled support among his colleagues for the rules in the bill: “There will be a lot of political pressure, in the wake of everything that’s happened, on the companies to actually do a very good job of the geographic validation of where the chip actually is.”
Ten years after AlphaGo’s match against Go champion Lee Sedol, today’s AI still isn’t tapping into the machinery that made that win possible.

When the Chip Security Act was introduced, in May 2025, lawmakers said the technology to implement it existed, something Nvidia has not publicly confirmed.
